fields.summary: Qt should have a class to represent a period of time

issuetype.description: Public suggestions
issuetype.name: Suggestion

customfield_10020.name: PM Spotted
customfield_10020.goal: PM tracking of issue with potential concern or priority. Needs further clarification

content.text: Dealing with durations could be a lot easier if Qt had a class to represent that.
To make this possible, we created a patch for Qt that realizes this for which we request a merge:
http://qt.gitorious.org/qt/qt/merge_requests/1014
This is just a Jira issue to make it easier to track this request and get it to the right people.
This report is linked to this older request for QPeriod:
I am not convinced of the usefullness of this class in Qt.
Anyone to convince me?

What would it take to convince you, other than the arguments already made in the merge request, the mailing list discussions and DevNet topic linked there, the earlier suggestion for this functionality made, and the fact that this managed to get 19 votes in just a week or two?

I think it would be useful, and so do a lot of others, it seems. Compare it with QRect (some QTimeSpan methods are actually modelled on it): it is possible to just use two QPoints whenever you need a rect, but it is more convenient to have a QRect. The same goes for QTimeSpan: sure, you can reimplement it every time you need it (and make all the mistakes that come with that), or you do it once and add it to a library.
I at least find that I need a class like this regularly, and it seems to me so do more people.
Indeed, why have QVector, QPointF, QVector2d, QPair? Convenience and they each have their own API specifics for domain specific functionality. QTimeSpan is no different in that respect.
Perhaps it would convince you if you know that competing frameworks like .Net does offer this functionality?
Actually mentioning that ".Net" has this feature makes very little difference. I just commented the merge request, there are still some points that need to be discussed.
The discussion for this is happening in the merge request itself.
Whatever happened to this ticket?
Seems it got lost over time as it was unassigned. Maybe Thiago can say something.

The code is rotting in a repository somewhere. Problem was that each time I wanted to work on it again, it basically got stalled because other major work on the time/date stuff was going on or announced. I still think it would be useful (and I still use the current code for time to time, very recently the last time), but I do think that perhaps it needs to work differently than it does now.
It would of course be good if you could move the code over to codereview, especially as gitorious is about to be shut down.
I am not sure of the value of this class. If you're going to represent just a period of time, use the std::chrono classes. Add support for them in our API wherever necessary instead.
So we can add dependencies on std in the public Qt API now? I had the impression that we could not, but I may be mistaken then.
You cannot.
But since all of the chrono API is templated, there won't be any ABI impact.
To detect if chrono API is available:

#ifdef __has_include
#  if __has_include(<chrono>)
...
#  endif
#endif
Compilers before Clang 3.5 and GCC 5 will not be supported.
Any progress with this?
: about using std::chrono - it does not, AFAIK, provide utilities for parsing/printing durations, in formats such as
1 year 2 months 3 days 4 hours 5 minutes 6 seconds
, or
for example.
There are interesting examples how time intervals, as PostgreSQL names them, can be formated here:
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/datatype-datetime.html#DATATYPE-INTERVAL-INPUT-EXAMPLES
Was this addressed by
http://doc-snapshots.qt.io/qt5-dev/qdeadlinetimer.html
No, QDeadlineTimer roughly compares to the proposed class like QTimer does to QDateTime.
QDeadlineTimer is like std::chrono::time_point, not std::chrono::duration. And no parsing and representation in string format.
Any progress on this?
no.
Sadly the linked qt.gitorious.org site is long gone, so I can't look at what was originally offered.
I note that "a period of time" can mean
the period from a specified start-point to a specified end-point (possibly described by a duration and one end-point) or
a duration, at no specified time.
The former is what a calendar app attaches an appointment to.
The latter is a "time diff".  This request appears to be for the latter.
We should be able to add
QDateTime::add(std::chrono::duration)
without much trouble, which would provide the "time-diff" aspect.  (I am not a fan of C++20's
std::chrono::months
duration,
days; it won't do what the user expects, as
.add(std::chrono::months(1) + std::chrono::days(3))
shall not agree with
.addMonths(1).addDays(3)
.  We might plausibly be able to have
add()
notice when what it's passed is a
std::chrono::months(N)
and treat it as
.addMonths(N)
, but arithmetic with a finer duration type will make a nonsense of that.  Indeed,
std::chrono::years
shall present similar problems.)
Thiago mentions parsing, representation and string format.
Those
appear to be
missing from
std::chrono::duration
, although it supports literals in code with well-defined format; I imagine we would want to support string formats such as
"1yr 3day 4h 5min 6s 789ms 210us 543ns"
, although I imagine the literal format would require
in the gaps between parts.  Then again, we have to consider how we would localize that.
What other features of a duration in time were intended ?

The class we proposed originally offered a duration, with an optional "anchor" point in time. If it had an anchor point, it would have more capabilities like formatting a difference as "1 year, 2 months and 4 days".

It also offered support for things like substracting two QDate(Time) objects, yielding a QTimeSpan, and for adding a QTimeSpan to a QDate(Time) yielding a new QDate(Time) offset by the duration of the time span. Some of this would still be useful I think, but I would not implement it again the way I did back in 2011.
Still, for those interested, the sources still float around on the internet (and some even claim it as their own, unfortunately
). For instance:
https://github.com/a1batross/plasma-widget-ponycountdownplasma/blob/master/qtimespan.h
https://github.com/a1batross/plasma-widget-ponycountdownplasma/blob/master/qtimespan.cpp
Maybe it is a time to give QTimeSpan give another try at code review?
Unfortunately, std::chrono::duration does not cover the required functionality expectations.
So
QTimeSpan

is a hybrid of what I'd describe as duration and interval; if the optional anchor date is left off, it's a duration, but with the anchor it's an interval.  My first inclination would be to separate the two, but the reasoning around handling of months and years does provide a reason for the conflation (closely related to my objections to
std::chrono
's
months
and
years
, above).  I shall need to read the rationale behind the
std::chrono::duration
design, I think.

I would like to work on that. Seems like a not so high level task to make a first code contribution. Would it be fine to grab the old code which is floating around on github, pushing it to gerrit and give the discussion a new start there, with code in place to get discussed?
You can submit any code you own copyright for or any code a third party already submitted to Qt via Gerrit (htps://codereview.qt.io). Anything else you can't submit to Qt.
I would be wiling to figure out a way for you (
) to be able to take it over, and I'm pretty sure it won't be hard to convince Sean to also sign off on that.
Sure, it's fine by me.
According to
, it might still be not suitable for me to directly push it to gerrit because it never has been put there by its original authors?
You can push to Gerrit anything that you wrote or anything that has been pushed to Gerrit.
If it's elsewhere on the Internet, then it needs to have a proper licence file with a very permissive licence (ISC, MIT, BSD) and you need to put it in src/3rdparty.
This applies to everyone, not just non-Qt Company people.
How about I push it to Gerrit as a WIP, and you
pick it up from there? That would be ok licence wise, right
Yes.
it's been a while. Have you been able to push it already?
On the right of this page there's a panel with sections for People, Dates, Agile, Slack and Gerrit Reviews.
If there were a review in gerrit for this, that includes a
Task-number:
or
Fixes:
footer referencing this bug, it would show up in the last.  As there isn't, I guess
doesn't yet have it ready for review (or is missing a footer; see the Qt project's standard new commit message template).
Well,
of course there are always requirements to met. What I do not fully understand is, that
obviously pushed it to gitorious years ago as a merge request. Can't that get simply taken from the archive and pushed into gerrit without further interaction by the original author?
The situation is kind of an unsatisfying deadlock. I definitely want to contribute, but lack the skill to start the feature from scratch, but there is code around that
wrote and he stated several times that he is willing to let someone else work on it.
I would appreciate any legally possible solution that helps to make progress here.
You can clone
's github repo.  You can clone qtbase.  You can copy from the former to the latter,
git add
the result,
git commit
and push to gerrit.  If you ask your clone of the github repo for the
git log
history of the files you copied, you'll be able to find
's commit message to re-use it, along with
--author
, to preserve the original form, even.  You'll need
's permission to do that, of course; his comments above sound like he'll be sympathetic to your doing this.
In the mean time std::chrono::duration has filled that gap; is a Qt class still needed to represent time durations?
Yeah, I think
std::chrono::duration
suffices now. There's even a way to format it to strings using
std::format
There are two meanings of "time interval" or "period of time": one, that
std::chrono::duration

represents, is just the temporal size of the interval, for example "three hours"; the other has a start-time and an end-time, with a duration of the first kind as the difference between them, for example "a one hour meeting starting at 10:00".
The latter is quite important in calendars, as you might guess from that example.
I can't access the gitorious link above now, so I don't know which of the two the reporter wanted; but if it was the "from start-moment to end-moment" type it isn't covered by
std::chrono::duration
, so feel free to reopen.

fields.summary: QtConcurrent::mapped doesn't work with C++11 lambdas

issuetype.description: A user story for the product
issuetype.name: User Story

content.text: QtConcurrent::mapped currently supports function pointers, pointer to member-functions, and functors which define a nested typedef result_type as map and reduce functions. Lambda expressions don't have that typedef, so compilation fails.

Workaround: stateless lambdas decay into function pointers, so you use the dereference operator to make them into function references, which again decay to function pointers, to force a function pointer deduction:
<code>
auto result = QtConcurrent::blockingMapped(someList, *[=](ListItem item){ return QString(""); });
QtConcurrent should not require result_type nested typedefs.
Confirmed. Unit tests (which don't compile) attached.
I attached an
unacceptable_patch.diff
which uses a horrible homegrown trait to find the return type, instead of requiring
result_type
. I dug that trait out of this SO answer:
https://stackoverflow.com/a/27823546/252857
. Note that it's lacking specializations for
nothrow
noexcept
A proper fix would need to be more elegant, so this is mostly as a challenge for someone to find a better way (I haven't so far)
That's C++17
noexcept
overload, not
nothrow
See
https://qt-project.atlassian.net/browse/QTBUG-22710
. Does mapped() work with a lambda if you pass in the right type as a template argument?
Does not seem like it does. I think this is a different issue.
Ah yes, corrected.
I guess the trait in the patch I attached could be shortened a bit using
std::remove_cv
and
std::remove_reference
. But still, would be nice with a better approach. I first thought
std::result_of
could be used somehow (deprecated in C++17 in favor of
std::invoke_result)
, but I do not think it works with lambdas ( ? ) :/
Can you show me how you provided the template argument, and what the compiler error is when trying to do that?
Well I think it's simply not possible since, unless I'm mistaken, unlike for
mappedReduced
, the
ResultType
is not a template argument for the
mapped
function.
E.g. trying to do what you did in
with
mapped
, I get:

[estan@newton conctest]$ make
g++ -c -pipe -O2 -Wall -W -D_REENTRANT -fPIC -DQT_DEPRECATED_WARNINGS -DQT_NO_DEBUG -DQT_GUI_LIB -DQT_CONCURRENT_LIB -DQT_CORE_LIB -I. -I. -isystem /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5 -isystem /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5/QtGui -isystem /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5/QtConcurrent -isystem /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5/QtCore -I. -isystem /usr/include/libdrm -I/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5/mkspecs/linux-g++ -o conctest.o conctest.cpp
conctest.cpp: In function ‘int main(int, char**)’:
conctest.cpp:6:63: error: no matching function for call to ‘mapped<int>(QList<int>&, main(int, char**)::<lambda(int)>)’
     QtConcurrent::mapped<int>(list, [](int v) { Q_UNUSED(v); });
                                                               ^
In file included from /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5/QtConcurrent/QtConcurrentMap:1:0,
                 from conctest.cpp:2:
/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5/QtConcurrent/qtconcurrentmap.h:177:74: note: candidate: template<class Sequence, class MapFunctor> QFuture<typename QtPrivate::MapResultType<void, MapFunctor>::ResultType> QtConcurrent::mapped(const Sequence&, MapFunctor)
 QFuture<typename QtPrivate::MapResultType<void, MapFunctor>::ResultType> mapped(const Sequence &sequence, MapFunctor map)
                                                                          ^~~~~~
/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5/QtConcurrent/qtconcurrentmap.h:177:74: note:   template argument deduction/substitution failed:
conctest.cpp:6:63: note:   cannot convert ‘list’ (type ‘QList<int>’) to type ‘const int&’
     QtConcurrent::mapped<int>(list, [](int v) { Q_UNUSED(v); });
                                                               ^
In file included from /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5/QtConcurrent/QtConcurrentMap:1:0,
                 from conctest.cpp:2:
/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5/QtConcurrent/qtconcurrentmap.h:184:74: note: candidate: template<class Iterator, class MapFunctor> QFuture<typename QtPrivate::MapResultType<void, MapFunctor>::ResultType> QtConcurrent::mapped(Iterator, Iterator, MapFunctor)
 QFuture<typename QtPrivate::MapResultType<void, MapFunctor>::ResultType> mapped(Iterator begin, Iterator end, MapFunctor map)
                                                                          ^~~~~~
/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/qt5/QtConcurrent/qtconcurrentmap.h:184:74: note:   template argument deduction/substitution failed:
conctest.cpp:6:63: note:   candidate expects 3 arguments, 2 provided
     QtConcurrent::mapped<int>(list, [](int v) { Q_UNUSED(v); });
                                                               ^
Makefile:561: recipe for target 'conctest.o' failed
make: *** [conctest.o] Error 1
[estan@newton conctest]$
This is because
mapped
has parameters
template <typename Sequence, typename MapFunctor>
, unlike
mappedReduced
which has
template <typename ResultType, typename Sequence, typename MapFunctor, typename ReduceFunctor>
I think I'd have to pass in all template paramters (i.e. the full
SequenceType
and
MapFunctor
type, which in the case of a lambda I think is gnarly).

So, aside from the fact that the documentation contains contradictory statements right now, what, exactly, is the problem? Obtaining the return type of a generic callable (provided it is not overloaded, at least!) is totally achievable. Even assuming the standard library doesn't already have a suitable utility, or that it can't be used for whatever reason, it's hardly impossible for Qt to roll its own.
I've done so in
https://github.com/Kitware/kwiver/blob/master/vital/range/defs.h
(see
function_detail
). Live demo proving it works on stateful lambdas:
https://godbolt.org/z/fZdQq1
. It should be possible to just replace the current brain-dead implementation of
QtPrivate::MapResultType

with that... (I'd also encourage renaming that helper at the same time to something more generic!) Probably this could even replace the (broken) fallback version of that (i.e. for functors that don't have a
result_type
) while retaining the existing implementation, which would maintain compatibility and provide an escape hatch for users that for some reason need to pass in something with overloaded
operator()
Your
function_detail

looks similar to the trait in the diff I attached, except the one I posted handles a few more cases I think (I can't take credit for it though as a I found it on SO). The diff also has a little test case showing it'll work with stateful lambdas. The reason I named the patch
unacceptable_patch.diff

is that I asked Thiago beforehand on IRC whether a solution like that would be acceptable, and he said he'd only consider it if was done using traits from the standard library, not if it involved home grown traits.
I tried to find some way of using
std::result_of
invoke_result
since C++17), but couldn't find any. I didn't try that hard though.
Um... I took another look at this, and I think we may both be trying way too hard. I think this may be as simple as:
No
result_of
invoke_result
or other complicated helpers needed...
I've attached
that shows an incomplete proof-of-concept. A "full" version would need to find and adjust everywhere that QtPrivate::MapResultType is used as well as places that incorrectly use
MapFunctor::result_type
directly, and should add tests using lambdas to all relevant functions.
I'm not sure how to best handle
LazyResultType
; I suppose for compatibility, we still want to use
MapFunctor::result_type
if it exists, but doing so requires that
LazyResultType

also takes an argument list, which is awkward to do as a direct parameter pack due to the deduced template parameter. (Although, having it take exactly one argument would solve this problem, at a loss of generality.)
If that could work that would be great.
What do you think of Matthew's approach?
To be clear... I only fiddled with Qt's code enough to get my own code to work¹, but my code
did
compile and run with my patch. Accordingly, I'm willing to claim that it does work. I'm not sure if I will try to complete it or not, but we should agree on how to handle `LazyResultType` first.
(¹ Okay, maybe a
little
more than that, but it's still definitely not a complete patch; my goal was to show that the approach is feasible.)

items.fromString: The "function" parameter of QtConcurrent::mapped is of type MapFunction, which generally is the dereference result of a function pointer. So with lambda expression, I need to write the following: auto result = QtConcurrent::blockingMapped(someList, *[=](ListItem item){ return QString(""); }); While everywhere in Qt, even in QtConcurrent::run, the star sign "*" before the lambda expression is not needed. The function parameter should be changed to funtion pointer or similar stuff to keep consistence with the standard function pointer way.
items.toString: QtConcurrent::mapped currently supports function pointers, pointer to member-functions, and functors which define a nested typedef result_type as map and reduce functions. Lambda expressions don't have that typedef, so compilation fails. Workaround: stateless lambdas decay into function pointers, so you use the dereference operator to make them into function references, which again decay to function pointers, to force a function pointer deduction: auto result = QtConcurrent::blockingMapped(someList, *[=](ListItem item){ return QString(""); }); QtConcurrent should not require result_type nested typedefs.

items.fromString: QtConcurrent::mapped should use function pointer as MapFunction

content.text: Currently undo framework is under widgets but it would be useful in other areas too. Such as console and QML/QtQuick based applications.
Related discussions:
https://lists.qt-project.org/pipermail/development/2011-December/000932.html
https://lists.qt-project.org/pipermail/development/2012-February/thread.html#1818
(later continuation of the above)
https://lists.qt-project.org/pipermail/development/2017-April/029382.html
Related patches:
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/15857
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/190704
Note that QUndoView should stay in QWidgets, of course. Only the core of Undo framework should more to a more general module...
+1. I think this would be really useful to have in Qt GUI, though I'm curious how that would work, given QAction's reliance on widgets...
That was fun!
https://github.com/mitchcurtis/qt-undo
It's not 100% done yet, but it works; it just needs polish.
https://codereview.qt-project.org/#/c/222371/
exposes more properties of QUndoStack. QUndoCommand should be made a
Q_GADGET
in Qt 6 so that Qt Quick applications that need to show a list of named undoable commands can do so via the
text
property.

content.text: Using Material style from qt.labs.controls I'm able to set primary and accent colors for nthe space between statusbar and navigation bar.
for good looking Material-style Android Apps it should be possible also to set the color of Android Status Bar (primary darker)
as documented here:
http://developer.android.com/training/material/theme.html#StatusBar
would be cool to make this possible.
There are probably several options:
as far as I remember, the status bar color can be set in AndroidManifest.xml
alternatively one could subclass QtActivity.java and set the color in Java
you can probably set the color in C++ too, using the QAndroidJni* classes from QtAndroidExtras
thx
will take a look at this.

I tried to set status bar color through manifest. When application starting, status bar has proper color, so it works. But then, it changes into black. Seems, Qt reset this color, or may be I do something wrong?
I added file android/res/values-v21/style.xml:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<resources>
  <style name="AppTheme" parent="android:Theme.Material">
    <item name="android:colorPrimaryDark">#455a64</item>
  </style>
</resources>
and added to manifest
android:theme="@style/AppTheme"
Tested on Qt 5.7 from git and AVD 5.7.
thx Nikita, that you're testing this.
I haven't found time yet because of heavy work on blog series about Qt 5.7 material style apps.
For me would be important to get the status bar colored.
It seems that the current code for QtActivity only accepts Android's own themes. I could get around it by extending QtActivity and doing this:
thx Leonardo, this will help for static value,
but as I understad it right won't help to dynamically set the statusbar color
per ex. as Google Play Store does
one of my enterprise customers always lets their employees select between two color schema, so I'm setting primary and accent color dynamically for existing BB10 apps -
and I would like to do this also from Qt 5.7 apps.
would be great to have an API
I see. I don't feel it suits Qt. It's such a platform specific feature... Well, never mind. It's just my opinion. In the meantime, you should try using the native java method:
https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/Window.html#setStatusBarColor(int)
That with a bit of JNI and you're done.
thx Leonardo.
will try it later. not so easy to figure it out for me coming from 4+ years intensive BlackBerry 10 Cascades (Qt 4.8/QML) development. I'm not an experienced Android developer
I managed to change the status bar color. First you need to extend the QtActivity.java. So, override the method onCreate as:
It works for me.
Hi Enoque,
and where you can find the QtActivity.java? I've just found the QtActivity.class.
Or you have to create it?
Thanks!
Hi Carles Sole Grau,
you can find in your Qt for Android installation, accessing the folder: Qt5.7.0/5.7/android_armv7/src/android/java/src/org/qtproject/qt5/android/bindings/QtActivity.java.
so,
1: create a java class that extends QtActivity.java;

I made a simple example app:

statusbar.h

// main.cpp
qmlRegisterType<StatusBar>("StatusBar", 0, 1, "StatusBar");

WOW!!
J-P Nurmi, thank you very much!
J-P, this is soooo cool
thx providing this - will make Qt Quick Controls 2 Apps look much better now.
WOW ! my old Bug from 2016 now is In Progress
remember coming from BlackBerry10/Cascades the first time with new Qt QuickControls2 and much help from J-P and Mitch
BTW: would be great not only to set the StatusBar color and Theme, but also on Android setting NavigationBar color and scheme

I'd like to clarify something here. We don't have an API in Qt to set the status bar or any other window system decoration colors to arbitrary colors, and we don't want that either i think, as it's not something we can do cross platform, AFAIK.
But the use-case on mobile to have a "colored statusbar" should be covered by the combination of

fields.summary: Provide a way to conveniently use test helper functions with qtestlib

issuetype.description: Public suggestions
issuetype.name: Suggestion

content.text: I have a helper class from which my test case derives from. The helper class sets up a bunch of stuff via non-test helper functions. I was using QVERIFY, QCOMPARE, etc. in those helper functions, until I realised that the test function keeps executing.
In the docs, each test function has this note:
Note: This macro can only be used in a test function that is invoked by the test framework.
This all makes sense, but it leaves a huge gap in implementing and using helper functions in tests.
My current workaround is to duplicate some of the macros:
I store a failureMessage string in the helper class:
const char *failureMessage;

I ensure that the result of the helper is used (they return bool so that the actual test function can verify that they succeed), and I give them a goofy prefix so that it's obvious that they're a helper:
Q_REQUIRED_RESULT bool helpDeleteSavedTestGames();
For example, the VERIFY macro returns false if it fails, and stores the failure message. The client code in the actual test functions uses the helper like so:
QVERIFY2(helpDeleteSavedTestGames(), failureMessage);
This has worked fine so far, but it uses private API, so it would be good if there was an official way to do this.
Consider sth like
https://codereview.qt-project.org/#/c/248244/
More cases:

In member function 'QImage tst_QQuickItemLayer::runTest(const QString&)':
tst_qquickitemlayer.cpp:54:37: warning: ignoring return value of 'bool QTest::qWaitForWindowExposed(QWindow*, int)', declared with attribute nodiscard [-Wunused-result]                      

tst_qquickmultipointtoucharea.cpp: In member function 'QQuickView* tst_QQuickMultiPointTouchArea::createAndShowView(const QString&)':
tst_qquickmultipointtoucharea.cpp:1155:33: warning: ignoring return value of 'bool QTest::qWaitForWindowExposed(QWindow*, int)', declared with attribute nodiscard [-Wunused-
A really bad example can also be seen in qtbase/tests/auto/widgets/util/qundostack/tst_qundostack.cpp.
A possible kludge would be
#define QTEST_CHECKED(...) do { __VA_ARGS__; if (QTest:currentTestFailed()) return; } while (false)
so that your test would
QTEST_CHECKED(helper(args));
(The use of macro var-args is so that you can equally
QTEST_CHECKED(helper<T, V>(t, v));
without the preprocessor barfing on the comma in
<T, V>
, which isn't enclosed in parentheses, so looks like a macro parameter separator to it.)
Would throwing and catching be an alternative to this, the way that e.g. Catch implements test failures in leaf functions?
That was what I was initially trying with my old patches, and what
is doing in
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/265652
That would require clients of
QTest
to enable exceptions, though; my understanding was that Qt tried to avoid imposing that.
QTEST_CHECKED

is simple, minimal, but it's annoying. The epic also mentions using exceptions to report failure, which wouldn't need such user-provided macros. And for the vast majority of test cases (those that don't spin up threads to qFail in them), the difference to the current implicit return would be rather undetectable.
As for exceptions being disabled: This comes up every time, but while we disable them for our own libraries (except QtCore), I have yet to see a testcase that has exceptions disabled.
And even if there were test cases with exceptions disabled, the macros could detect that and simply return instead of throw:
Where
The problem with a maybe-throw is that, when it doesn't throw, we're back in the same old boat of the macros only returning from the function that calls them, so their callers need to check
QTest::currentTestFailed()
, so tests that need to work without exceptions need something like
QTEST_CHECKED()
, used at every level in their call tree. But, indeed, adding support for letting the test use exceptions instead is worth doing, and it'll make for simpler test code (although it'll complicate
QTest
's own code).
The problem with a maybe-throw is that, when it doesn't throw, we're back in the same old boat of the macros only returning from the function that calls them, [...]

Yeah, well, "if you want to return from nested test functions, return enable exceptions, otherwise continue as before" is a pretty simple story to tell. So I wouldn't call it a problem. If you think it is, we can enforce exceptions for QTestLib use, too (by just using
throw
in inline code, though I'd prefer if we threw and caught in the same TU, so that the exception class can stay unexported.
Throwing would potentially also allow us more levels of test "functions", than the current suite+function, similar to the BDD mechanisms here:
https://github.com/catchorg/Catch2/blob/devel/docs/test-cases-and-sections.md#bdd-style-test-cases
Just to be clear, I'm not opposed to
adding
support for a throwing-based mechanism, just delineating the need for a non-throwing mechanism for those who build without exceptions; which is solved by
QTEST_CHECKED()
Over lunch,

made an interesting suggestion: we could simply have the existing macros initially check-and-return, before doing the checks they're defined for. This would solve the need for a separate call-and-check macro for the sub-functions (and would be analogous to
QTestEventLoop
exiting its loop early if it finds the test has failed).  I'll aim to look into the feasibility of that when I can find time – but don't let that stop others investigating first.
It also occurs to me that, in any case, what we should be checking for is not just failure but also "has the present test skipped", since we should also return early if a helper has called
QSKIP()
By the way, old discussion about this bug:
https://lists.qt-project.org/pipermail/development/2019-April/035552.html

I read the ML thread, and I remain unconvinced of the need to add a macro wrapping calls to helper subroutines to add context. The throw site, as well as the catch site should be in out-of-line code in QtTestLib, and so we can do all sorts of checks between the two, including
recording a backtrace at the point of throwing (the main work here is to figure out how to report that in the output, not the backtrace itself)
verifying that an exception that we threw makes it out the other end (catching catch-all-return misuses, albeit at runtime)
The helper macro is of value at least for those who do not enable exceptions.
It is also usable today by those who do have exceptions, for all that an exception-based solution would be better for them.

Meanwhile, the exception-based solution is still only at the point where we're all reasonably sure it can be done – at least in theory, assuming we don't stumble on some show-stopper we haven't thought of yet, that might mean it would entail a more drastic rearchitecting of testlib to make it possible – not at the point where I see someone with a working patch up for review on Gerrit.  (And, for reference, I am fairly sure those caveats about theory probably won't bite us: but until I see working code I won't know for sure.)
Should we abandon an improvement today for all users because we have dreams of a better solution that, at best, will only work for those who build with exceptions enabled ?
Should we abandon an improvement today for all users because we have dreams of a better solution that, at best, will only work for those who build with exceptions enabled ?
Yes.

We should de-risk that dream ASAP, instead of spending time on the temporary improvement. When we have de-risked the exception-based approach, we'll know whether to go ahead with the wrapper macros or not.
I do not understand the logic of that.  The macro is not only a temporary improvement for those who use exceptions; it is a permanent one for those who don't.  Why give that up ?
Because it's a solution in search of a problem.

We don't disable exceptions in test code, even though we do for most of our other code. We don't know whether there's a single user of QtTestLib that disables exceptions (manually, because neither the qmake nor the cmake magic does, AFAIU), and even if, how many of those use nested helper functions. This is such a small niche compared to doing the right thing and using exceptions that, IMHO, we shouldn't attempt to solve it before we solve the problem for the other 99% of users.
[fortunately I had your original text in a mail I hadn't yet deleted - edit reverted, sorry about that].
> Because it's a solution in search of a problem.
We literally have dozens of places where we were doing the thing this macro expands to.
This was a problem we already had, and had several vaguely similar approximations to this solution to it scattered through our tests.
So no, it was not a solution looking for a problem, it was a problem reported in our Jira and solved repeatedly in our own tests, that this solution formalises and unifies.
There is a better solution for an unquantifiable subset of Qt's users, that does indeed include us, but I have worked on a code-base in the past that
did
disable exceptions on the platforms where we used Qt, so I really don't think it's safe to take for granted that such client projects are non-existent.
We have dozens of places where we did this, compared to tens of thousands where we don't. I'm not saying that the macro isn't useful to
someone

. I'm saying that adding the macro before switching to exceptions is detrimental. The current trick with currentTestFailed() is not old and not widespread. Blessing it by adding a macro for it, and publicizing it in the ChangeLog, will drastically increase the number of users of this technique. Those will have to change their code when we switch to exceptions, and only those in the minority who disable exceptions won't.
I'm in particular talking about the follow-up patches where you're converting existing tests to use the new macro.

If, instead, we added the exception mechanism, then users would fall into the pit of success and do the right thing right away: just enable exceptions for the tests. All that's needed is that exceptions are enabled for QtCore (anyway the case), QtTestLib (tbc), and the test code itself (SEP).
If we
then

add the macro for those users that don't want to enable exceptions even in their test code, fine by me, but how does that square with QtTestLib throwing and catching exceptions? It would need to be compiled in two different forms: with and without exceptions. I really don't see why we'd need that additional complexity.
I very much agree with
on this one.
QTEST_CHECKED()
duly abandoned.
do you or anyone else in the core team have any interest in continuing
Giuseppe's patch

? The QTest::currentTestFailed workaround is helpful, but lacks the actual location of the call to the helper function in the failure message, which makes finding the higher-level place where the test failed really tedious.
Combining the lack of extra context for QCOMPARE when you're in a loop, and the lack of caller line number info for helpers, we end up with code like this:
With exceptions for macros and printf-style args for QCOMPARE, it could be something like this:
Doesn't look like much of a difference, but over the huge amounts of test code that is written, it is.
Edward Welbourne do you or anyone else in the core team have any interest in continuing Giuseppe's patch?
There may be interest, but I'm not sure when there shall be time.
I've added it to the (still finite) team backlog, maybe someone will pick it up.
Started implementing this as a hackathon project. Will add Task-number/Fixes to them.

content.text: This work document describes the ongoing work to port QStyle to QtQuick Controls 2, with the overall goal of improving support for writing desktop applications with a native Look-And-Feel.
Controls available, but missing native style (supported by QStyle)
TabBar
ToolButton (Button with menu)
ToolSeparator
Controls available, but missing native style (unsupported by QStyle)
Switch
RangeSlider
BusyIndicator
DelayButton
PageIndicator
Tumbler
Controls missing (compared to Qt Widgets)
TabView
cannot be composed as TabBar + StackView, it's has more combined visuals on e.g macOS
ScrollableTextArea (same concept as on macOS)
or improve support putting TextArea inside ScrollView
QToolBar
ToolBar (and side bar) should have a combined visual look on macOS
QFontComboBox
QTimeEdit
QDateEdit
QKeySequenceEdit
QMdiArea
QMdiSubWindow
QDockWidget
QToolBox
QCommandLinkButton
Line (in Qt Designer, which is a Frame. Integrate into ToolSeparator?)
Controls missing (compared to XCode IB)
Segmented button (mac) in controls1 as ButtonGroup/ButtonRow?
SearchField
Controls available, but with missing API (compared to Qt Widgets)
Small and Mini API for most controls
TextArea
BorderStyle. Important to be able to place it inside e.g a Frame or a ScrollView that already has a frame.
Putting it inside a ScrollView should just work
suffers from the same problems as with flickable above.
frameStyle (Shape, Shadow)
frameShape (Box, Panel, WinPanel, etc)
or perhaps borderStyle (border is more QML): (none, Line, bezel, rounded)
sborder style/frameShape (none, Line, bezel, rounded)
ScrollBar

Add API to specify if a scrollbar should be transient or not (fade away when not used). Currently a scrollbar is transient if the the policy is ScrollBar.AsNeeded. But this is different for a desktop style where the scrollbar should typically stay or hide depending on the content/viewport ratio, and not if it's being actively used. This should also control if the scrollbars are used as overlays in ScrollArea, or placed on the side of the contents.
On mac, work is needed to animate transient scrollbars.

On mac, the background should sometimes have a frame, other times not. But it looks like the stand-alone version should not have any frames. But when used in a NSScrollView, it should. So investigate more how to decide when to use a frame, and how to draw it.

If a flickable has both vertical and horizontal scrollbars, they overlap in the bottom-right corner. This looks wrong when the scrollbars have a background. A fix could be to resize the scrollbars differently when the background delegate is set/visible.
GroupBox
Checkable groupboxes (a checkbox can be placed in the groupbox title)
ToolButton
Missing a menu API. The button should be styled with an arrow if it opens a menu, so hacking this together from the app will probably not be enough?
Slider
Missing tick-marks API
Dial
Missing tick-marks API
Other things that needs to be done
Make "default" style be the platform style. And rename "default style" to e.g "plain style"
Adjust all layout rects, and verify that controls look as expected with layouts
Add cmake support
Add native menus/popups (for combobox, tooltip, etc)
Read QPlatformTheme
https://github.com/KDE/qqc2-desktop-style
Has the issue of having to link in Widgets just for QStyle

Something that is a bit related to desktop styling: You often expect to be able to copy non-editable text on desktops. This can currently only be done by making a non-editable text edit, but that does have some performance overhead and has a few more issues. The related issue for it was closed a year ago (
https://qt-project.atlassian.net/browse/QTBUG-14077
), but maybe this could be reconsidered if you want to have a more native feel on the desktop?
Just found this old task while going through all of them:
https://qt-project.atlassian.net/browse/QTBUG-67002
There was some interesting stuff mentioned about benchmarks and how "QStyle-rendered image blobs cripple the batch renderer". We should benchmark this and see how we're doing.
Interesting read. A couple of comments:

The native-style implementation only draw the backgrounds using QStyle, and not the foreground/text. And those images end up as nine-patch images that can be reused for all controls of the same type. This means that we e.g end up with one texture/material for all buttons, which can be batched by the renderer.
All images are placed in texture atlases. This means that we (should) end up with one material for drawing multiple controls (backgrounds). This again improves the possibility for batching.

We already follow this approach for the Imagine style, where we use pre-drawn background images. The only difference is with native-style we draw the images (mostly) at start-up, instead of loading them from disk/resources. And drawing textures from an atlas should be super-fast.

So I'm not concerned that this strategy "cripples the batch renderer". In fact, I think this strategy should be quite light-weight and fast, compared to styles like e.g Material that uses more advanced shaders . If we were to draw all controls with both background with foreground onto separate textures that couldn't be reused and scaled by the scene-graph (because of the foreground text), then it would be a completely different story. I assume this was the strategy used in Controls 1, and therefore also rightfully addressed in
Awesome, good to know.
And yes, I think the Material style is the slowest (although best-looking
) style we have.
Some of these controls can probably be done in plain QML, since they don't rely on QStyle styling.
Maybe we can take advantage of the Figma project for some of these controls?

As a first step, we duplicate the existing QStyle implementations from QtWidgets as a private API into QtQuickControls, and refactor it to not have any QWidget dependencies. Good if in the long run we don't have this duplication, but might not be realistic to have a unified architecture for both worlds.

Atlas-based style. Needs information about sizes, alignment, etc.

Investigate cascading.

QPainter-based and scenegraph-based. This also means text rendering.

Floating point based API.

 

*Current status:*

Missing widget controls in QQC2:
 * TabView (not only TabBar + StackView)
 * ScrollableTextArea (same concept as on macOS)
 * or improved support putting TextArea inside ScrollView

Native desktop controls missing in QQC2:
 * Segmented button (mac) in controls1 as ButtonGroup/ButtonRow?
 * SearchField

Controls in QQC2 that is not supported by QStyle:
 * Switch
 * RangeSlider
 * BusyIndicator
 * DelayButton
 * PageIndicator
 * Tumbler

Missing API and bugs:
 * Small and Mini controls API
 * TextArea
 ** BorderStyle. Important to be able to place it inside e.g a Frame or a ScrollView that already has a frame.
 ** Putting it inside a ScrollView should just work
 *** suffers from the same problems as with flickable above.
 ** frameStyle (Shape, Shadow)
 ** frameShape (Box, Panel, WinPanel, etc)
 *** or perhaps borderStyle (border is more QML): (none, Line, bezel, rounded)
 sborder style/frameShape (none, Line, bezel, rounded)
 * ScrollBar
 ** Add API to specify if a scrollbar should be transient or not (fade away when not used). Currently a scrollbar is transient if the the policy is ScrollBar.AsNeeded. But this is different for a desktop style where the scrollbar should typically stay or hide depending on the content/viewport ratio, and not if it's being actively used.
 ** On mac, work is needed to animate transient scrollbars.

 ** If a flickable has both vertical and horizontal scrollbars, they overlap in the bottom-right corner. This looks wrong when the scrollbars have a background. A fix could be to resize the scrollbars differently when the background delegate is set/visible.

Other things that needs to be done:
 * Adjust all layout rects, and verify that controls look as expected with layouts
 * Add cmake support
 * Add native menus/popups (for combobox, tooltip, etc)

fields.summary: Replace obsolete Keccak (sha3) implementation

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done
issuetype.name: Task

content.text: The Keccak implementation described by
sha3_keccak
in
qtbase/src/3rdparty/sha3/qt_attribution.json
appears to be the one that
Team Keccak
have
archived
under a "Warning! Below are obsolete packages and documents."  The same site
links to
diverse Free and Open Source implementations.  Presumably the archived version is deprecated in favour of these and we should upgrade to one of them.  This may also make the
sha3_endian
component (in the same directory) redundant.
None of the 10 evaluated sha3 implementations are completely satisfactory.
digestpp: Only supports little endian platforms.
tiny_sha3: Does not support keccak, only sha3. Only verified on little endian platforms.
DuSTman31/SHA3: Does not support intermediary hashes without modification, which is a requirement of QCryptographicHash.
Keccak-tiny: Can only hash in one step with all the data to hash in memory at the same time, hence not suitable for use by QCryptographicHash.
Libkeccak: Not C++ compatible without modifications.
SHA3IUF: Not C++ compatible without modifications. Sha3-224 support must be (trivially) added.
sha3sum: GPL license
fehashmac: GPL license
libmdigest: GPL license
XKCP: GPL license
I started a discussion in Qt/Platforms in Teams about support for big endian.
Libkeccak: Not C++ compatible without modifications.
What does that mean?
https://github.com/maandree/libkeccak
was active 13d ago, so it should be easy to upstream any changes that are required to make it compile as C++?
And what about libgcrypt? I thought is was under GPL, but it's actually LGPL (2.1+)
https://git.gnupg.org/cgi-bin/gitweb.cgi?p=libgcrypt.git;a=blob_plain;f=LICENSES;hb=HEAD
What does "compile as C++" even mean? We bundle Zlib, PCRE, XCB and I don't know how many C libraries – we just build them as C code and statically+privately link them into QtCore?
The present code (and the replacement currently in review) pulls in the 3rdparty SHA-3 code by a direct
#include
in
qcryptographichash.cpp
; I presume that's why
compilation is currently required.  That could be sorted out by changing how it's built, of course, but it is the path of least resistance !

In the case of Libkeccak, the only problems are inline functions in the libkeccak.h header where types are implicitly casted. This is one of the cases where C and C++ diverge. A commit to GitHub where the missing casts are added will probably be accepted.
Libgcrypt and crypto++ was not considered, but has a lot of functionality besides hashing functions. I'm not sure how they are affected by export regulations.
Random note: from a quick read of the manpages, libkeccak also seems to want to allocate memory (even
when hashing
, not sure what the deal is with that), and also the implementation is full of GCC-isms, aka no good for MSVC unless some good work™ is done on it.
Maybe we should start out with formulating explicit requirements?
For me, these would look like this:
(hard) Implemented in C or C++
(hard) can be fed data in chunks
(hard) does not allocate on addData()
(hard) does not allocate on finalize()
(soft) does not allocate on init()
(soft) has good pedigree
(soft) actively maintained
Feel free to add/subtract as you see fit, this is just a base for discussions.

Unlike OP, I don't think it's a problem to have an unmaintained upstream for this. The algorithms are set in stone, so what kind of changes do we expect upstream to make? C++ compile and warning fixes? Experience shows that we're likely hitting any of that sort way before upstream does. Security fixes? Maybe. We have Coverity running on the code, should check whether anything comes up, but the usual security issues with ciphers are more concerned with side-channel and timing attacks. Honestly, I don't think Qt can be used in application where these matter, and if it is, we have a contribution pending (
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/380034
) which uses a FIPS-certified library for
all
relevant hash algorithms, not just SHA3.
So, just leaving the old code is a completely valid approach, IMHO.
The only thing remaining is performance, but the same FIPS-certified library solution should get the optimised algorithms too. There's always AF_ALG on Linux too.

The problem with AF_ALG is that the actual hashers supported may vary at runtime, and we don't have that kind of API in QCryptographicHash, right? If we always need a fallback, then just use the fallback all the time.
(This also adds 8. to the list: compile-time knowledge that a given algorithm is available)

Libkeccak has a few libkeccak_zerocopy* functions which do not allocate. The libkeccak_zerocopy_update function can only handle buffer lengths of a multiple of libkeccak_zerocopy_chunksize, the rest has to be stored by the user and added in the libkeccak_zerocopy_digest call. This limitation is easy to handle.
We still have the problem that it uses a lot of internal gcc functions like __builtin_memset and similar, so it probably won't compile using MSVC.
There's however still the warning on finalize() (may allocate memory). I'm pretty sure that a non-allocating implementation could be added? I see no reason for that to allocate.
But then, do we want to commit to libkeccak and spend time improving/fixing it?
I think using AF_ALG as a linux specific optimization is separate task from this.
For this task we need algorithms that are always available on any platform.
It looks like all viable solutions requires some work from our side.
Only embedded systems would disable some AF_ALG algorithms and, in that case, you'll know when you run Qt and it crashes. Any generic Linux build will have all of them.

But indeed, the issue is that it's also a Linux-specific optimisation, so we need an alternative elsewhere. I think there's a Windows one, but its API is horrible for other reasons. No idea about Darwin.
As for the GCC builtins,

#ifdef Q_CC_MSVC
#  define __builtin_memset memset
#endif
XKCP: GPL license
This is inaccurate. It's CC0 + BSD (at least for the parts that interest us).
I'm still wondering if the replacement brings any value whatsoever at this point, instead of just reverting to what we had.
A single file in XKCP "
[support/Kernel-PMU/enable_arm_pmu.c|https://github.com/XKCP/XKCP/blob/master/support/Kernel-PMU/enable_arm_pmu.c]" is GPL.
If we can leave it out then there is no license problem.

Regarding libkeccak, the main header file contains inline functions with implicit void pointer casts, and the maintainer is unwilling to make it C++ compatible. He says he does not write polyglot code. It also requires the unix specific header file unistd.h which is not provided by MSVC, and he also uses some gcc specific functions, though some macros are defined on non-gcc platforms to call the standard C functions.
So, one language (C), one platform (Unix compatible ones), and one compiler (gcc).
So I'm abandoning work integrating with libkeccak.
Yes, reverting seems to be the best choice.
For reference, there was a mailing list discussion about deprecation of Keccak here:
https://lists.qt-project.org/pipermail/development/2019-June/036603.html
That discussion is only about the Keccak algorithm though, we still need sha-3.

XKCP is not usable either, because it uses uint8_t pointers in the interfaces, instead of (unsigned) char pointers. Reinterpret casting to uint8_t pointers violates strict aliasing rule, and is undefined behavior. It will work on most platforms, because uint8_t is usually type defined to a character type, but it is not portable or standard conformant code.
No usable replacement SHA-3 algorithm has been found. Stopping work on replacing the implementation. We will have to maintain the current implementation ourselves.
Huh?
uint8_t
is
unsigned char
. It's also the
defintiion
of byte, so strict aliasing rules do not apply: bytes can alias anything. That's how
memcpy
is allowed to exist.
Technically speaking, uint8_t could be a typedef to
any
type, incl. a magic implementation defined 8 bit extended integer type, which would therefore be wrong to use to access an object's representation as bytes.
Using int8_t for this purpose is therefore
idiomatically
wrong – in C (where you'd use unsigned char) as well as C++ (where you'd use std::byte, or char or unsigned char before C++20).
But well, we can easily shove yet another static_assert in qglobal.cpp to double check that on any platform we care about uint8_t exists and is precisely unsigned char, and we'd be good to go.
Yes, strictly speaking, it could. But doesn't in any platform known, much less those supported by Qt. It's always char or unsigned char.
Where did the signed int8_t come up?
Sorry, I meant, using uint8_t (unsigned) is idiomatically wrong. Likely it's aliased to unsigned char, so it's fine in both C and C++. We can turn the "likely" into a "certainly" via a static_assert.
uint8_t
, if it exists,
is
the size of and has the alignment of a byte. There's no exception to this rule.
The only question is whether it
is
unsigned char
or whether it's another integer type of the same size, alignment, and behaviour, but which may not have the correct aliasing rules.
The chance of that being the case is less than 0.01%, because it would break far too much C code.

fields.summary: Option to sort attributes in QDomDocument::toString()

issuetype.description: Public suggestions
issuetype.name: Suggestion

customfield_10020.name: Foundation PM Prioritized
customfield_10020.goal: This sprint is never started and serves as collection basked for grooming and prioritised issues. Vladimir owns the ordering.

content.text: Saving a QDomDocument to file sometimes results in its elements' attributes being reordered.
.e.g. the XML attributes in this QString:

<root name="fred">
    <element1 c="a" d="b" f="c"/ >
</root>
get reordered to:

<root name="fred" >
    <element1 f="c" c="a" d="b" />
</root>
I know that similar bugs were reported before and I have read them.
The previous reasons to not consider attribute order was optimization.

Instead of changing the default behavior, I propose adding an another option: a method or flag that makes it possible to save XML files with ordered attributes. Application developers would be able to choose whether they need it or not.
Rationale

Even if the XML standard does not care about the order of attributes, people may care. It is true that there are tools for comparing XML files, but XML is not only machine-readable. People sometimes need to read XML too, which is why
we already have options for pretty printing XML and JSON
. We even have options to change the size of indentation in XML, e.g. "
QDomDocument::toString(int indent = 1)
XML can be tracked in SCM (for example, Git), and random rearrangments produce useless large diffs.
Qt6?
It seems that Qt5 is at the end of its improvement period. Qt6 is on the roadmap, and I think it would be a good idea to introduce this feature before Qt6 is released.
I want to help and can prepare patches if this feature request is approved.
My two cents: I agree that this would be a beneficial feature (if not in Qt5, then hopefully in Qt6).
In
, the rationales for
not
implementing consistently-ordered attributes were as follows:
1. Order of attributes is meaningless.
...the DOM specification...states that the order of attributes has no meaning, [therefore] there is
no reason
for Qt to respect the order of the attributes. [Emphasis added.]
Reference here?
Extensible Markup Language (XML) 1.1 (Second Edition)
, section 3.1:
Start-Tags, End-Tags, and Empty-Element Tags
Note that the order of attribute specifications in a start-tag or empty-element tag is not significant.
Which may be true for machines generally, but as
mentioned, the order of attributes
does

have meaning for humans and version control systems, for example. (XML is intended to be human-readable as well as machine-readable, is it not?)  Isn't that a valid reason to maintain a consistent order of attributes in
QDomDocument
2. Implementation would hurt performance.
...it would mean that the internal representation of the attributes would need to change and this would have a performance hit as a result.
I'm a noob, but I'm guessing that's here in
src/xml/dom/qdom_p.h
QMultiHash<QString, QDomNodePrivate *> map;
From the documentation on
container classes
...if order doesn't matter
QHash
is a faster alternative (to
QMap
I assume this is due to the use of a hash table? And I assume that, by extension,
QMultiHash
is also faster than
QMultiMap
for that reason? But even though a hash table might be
generally
faster, I think an XML attribute list would be a rather specific application of a hash table – one that might be an exception to that general rule?
In
cited
QMap vs. QHash: A small benchmark
of lookups, which found that:
QMap is FASTER than QHash in the case that there are less than 20 entries (which imho will be true for most [XML] applications).
If so, then it suggests that performance might
improve
in many cases for a QDomDocument implemented with QMultiMap instead of QMultiHash.  (And FWIW, the interface to
QMultiMap
looks very similar to that of
QMultiHash
– it might even be a drop-in replacement?)

So why do you think QMulteMap will retain your 'order' (whatever this is)? It will only sort the attributes by key so your attributes are sorted alphabetically. But this is as wrong as not sorting them at all. And as you already wrote - the order is not defined by the standard so we don't need to care either.
Good points,
– in re-reading my earlier comment, I see that I didn't explain myself very well, so please allow me to clarify.
So why do you think QMulteMap will retain your 'order' (whatever this is)? It will only sort the attributes by key so your attributes are sorted alphabetically.
Yes, exactly.  For my part, I'm not concerned with
in which
order the attributes are sorted – only that the attributes are sorted
consistently
(in whatever order that happens to be, whether alphabetical or otherwise), rather than in a random order that
changes every time
; and I think having them sorted alphabetically would be the perfect solution.  (But I see that's not stated explicitly...perhaps the OP meant that they want the ability to sort the attributes in a
custom/user-defined
order?  If so, then I have misinterpreted the original report.)
And as you already wrote - the order is not defined by the standard so we don't need to care either.
Right, but my point (and the OP's point, I think) is that
despite
the standard, consistent order is still useful for (A) human readability, and (B) storage in version control systems; so for those reasons, IMHO we
should
care about the order of attributes,
even though
it's not required by the standard.  Thus the OP's suggestion to provide an optional implementation that
does
maintain a consistent order of attributes, for those applications that would benefit from it – surely there is value in such a feature?

I'd add point (C) - any form of deterministic testing is hindered by non-ordered attributes (example - storing reference XMLs and simple diff with generated ones). Although one could use qSetGlobalQHashSeed in tests it is not an obvious solution and has global impact, which would make the test less representative.
Isn't this fixed now?
I would say yes.

content.text: QDoc's auto-linker is slightly too eager to resolve link targets after the comment file feature; linking to even targets that are marked \internal.
Most prominent is the word 'macOS', where we tried to disable the autolinking by introducing an internal \externalpage. For example;

-

With the MySQL driver, it is possible to connect to a MySQL server. In order to build the QMYSQL Plugin for Unix or macOS, you need the MySQL header files as well as the shared library, libmysqlclient.so. To compile the plugin for Windows, install MySQL.

+

With the MySQL driver, it is possible to connect to a MySQL server. In order to build the QMYSQL Plugin for Unix or macOS, you need the MySQL header files as well as the shared library, libmysqlclient.so. To compile the plugin for Windows, install MySQL.
notice the macOS, which obviously is not intended.
Hi, we've encountered this bug in Qbs, e.g. see
https://qbs.io/docs/installing/
We have marked macOS as \internal (
https://github.com/qbs/qbs/blob/master/doc/external-resources.qdoc#L128
) but apparently it has no effect. Also, how's the issue is fixed if the gerrit change is abandoned and no commits are linked?

fields.summary: Equip QDateTime to distinguish the two passes through an "overlap" hour during a time-zone fall-back, such as the end of DST

issuetype.description: A user story for the product
issuetype.name: User Story

content.text: While
QDateTime

can map a UTC time to a local time, or time in some specified zone, in the overlap period of a zone transition, and will know which repeat of the time it represents (to the degree that it has the right offset from UTC, and will give the right time-zone if
toString()

is called with a suitable format) , we provide no way to indicate which repeat to use when constructing a time in this interval.  The existing implementation will pick one of them; the user can check its
isDaylightTime()
and
addSecs(60 * 60)
(or minus that) to fix it up, but there should be a way to tell the constructor which repeat to use, when the specified time happens twice.
Python's
datetime
objects

handle this using a "fold" parameter, set to 0 to get the first pass and 1 to get the second; this also affects handling of times in the gap when a time-zone transition skips an hour (as at the start of DST);
PEP495
specifies the full semantics.  In general,
fold=0
selects the UTC offset in effect before the transition while
fold=1
selects the offset in effect after the transition.  I propose to add a parameter with the same semantics.
The one work-around to the present deficiency relies on knowing the zone's offsets before and after the transition.  You can then construct a date-time object using
OffsetFromUTC
at the right offset and use
toTimeZone(zone)
or
toLocalTime()
to convert it to the zone whose transition is falling back just then.
Just for reference:
C++ 20 uses an enum, std::chrono::choose with the two options "earliest" and "latest". It uses it for both the gap at beginning of DST and the fold at the end.
https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/chrono/choose
I can think of several potential resolutions, around different questions:
Prefer a date-time { before | after } the transition
Respect time-difference from times { before | after } the transition
Prefer { Daylight-Saving | Standard } time

These all work differently. One may also, in handling date-times that hit a gap, opt (as we do at present) for a time the gap's width earlier or later than the one requested, or for a closest representable time at the gap's boundaries,  the last before, the first after or the one that a naive reading of the requested time would call closest. The result of any of these resolutions may be returned (as at present) as a
QDateTime
whose
isValid()
is false but whose
toMSecsSinceEpoch()
represents a date-time selected by the other options in play; or as a valid date-time selected by those options.
Let's try to decompose that into orthogonal questions:
In gap
In fold
Description
before
before
Prefer before
after
after
Prefer after
after
before
Respect diff from before
before
after
Respect diff from after
after
before
Prefer DST (if DST +ve)
before
after
Prefer Standard (if DST +ve)

The last two are swapped in a zone with negative DST; so the preference between DST and standard time is the same as respecting difference from before and after, one way round in a +ve DST zone, the other in a -ve DST zone.
So I think the answer is to have a
QFlag enum
with bits for gap / fold to be before / after, and perhaps some other bits for more esoteric details.
Then some pre-cooked combinations of those can have user-friendly-ish names.
Historical note: trawling my mail archive for other reasons I stumbled on my first brush with these issues,
How does mktime() handle DST transitions ?
Meanwhile some folk are
proposing a revision
to ECMA 262 that would replace JS's
Date
(which all parties, including the original author, admit is a bad design) with a new top-level object (similar to
Math
Temporal
, that provides more comprehensive services. Its design is worth understanding.
For the resolutions of times in transitions, see
Resolving Time Ambiguity in Temporal
That has a
disambiguation
parameter that can be
'reject'
(raise exception if in a transition),
'compatible'
(use the zone offset in effect before the transition) or the obvious pair of
'earlier'
'later'
to select between the two candidates resolutions.
These are covered, respectively, by
Reject
MatchTimeSince
PreferBefore
and
PreferAfter
in the present
QDateTime::TransitionOption
(The same spec
also has
an
offset
parameter for use when parsing a date-time that includes both an offset and the time-zone – in Qt time formats,
"ttt[tttt]"
would write or parse this – which may be worth taking into account when reinventing the date-time parser.)
Thanks to
for bringing this to my attention.
Blocked by QTBUG-108199; without a simplification of
QDateTime
APIs such as this provides, the changes needed to support transition control get too unwieldy.
is now fixed, so unblocked.
Failed to make 6.5 FF, so changed Fix Version to
[edit, 2023-10-19: finally landed in 6.7.]

fields.summary: Move Public Suffix List, QUrl::topLevelDomain to Qt Network

issuetype.description: A user story for the product
issuetype.name: User Story

content.text: Public Suffix list should be QtNetwork private API. It is mostly used by Cookie Jar in QtNetworking.
Deprecate in Qt 5.15
So what is the replacement for
QUrl::topLevelDomain()
It's useful for custom subclasses of
QNetworkCookieJar
etc.
Apparently, nobody cares. "topLevelDomain" is critically needed for some operations - for example any kind of AdBlocking functionalities etc.
Could ANYBODY enlighten us why this change was actually needed? WHY WHY WHY WHY.
I made my own very simplistic implementation, see
https://github.com/martinrotter/rssguard/blob/version-4/src/librssguard/network-web/urltld.cpp
It loads publis suffix list (
https://publicsuffix.org/list)
from Qt resource, parses it and then performs searching with it.
Use method
static QString topLevelDomain(const QUrl& url)
for finding TLD of an URL.
Could ANYBODY enlighten us why this change was actually needed? WHY WHY WHY WHY.

I was lobbying for this change because I think the data doesn't belong into Qt Core. Keep in mind Qt Core is the basis of every Qt application; I don't think it's sensible to let each console and desktop application pay the price in terms of data size, and well as third-party license documentation (the original data is available under Mozilla Public License Version 2.0), for a functionality that is of use only in term of network cookies.

Also keep in mind that, especially if you're using the publicsuffix list for security relevant things, you might rather look into getting the data directly from the source. We do only update the list from times to times, and not for every patch version. So if you're not always using the latest and greatest Qt version, the list is by definition already quite outdated ...
However, I see that for not-so-critical use cases, keeping the public suffix list in Qt is useful. So I think moving the data to Qt Network is a good compromise.
, moving is fine, the issue is that it is no longer public, unless something changed recently.
I agree that it is very useful to have it available in public API.

There is libpsl C library that can replace it, but it has heavy dependencies - either ICU of libidn2+libunistring+libiconv. That's not a problem if you build for Linux using system libraries, but more of a pain on Windows. ICU is extremely large dependency and it is not really necessary on Windows (AFAIK official binary builds of Qt don't even include it) so it will heavily inflate binary size. libidn2+libunistring+libiconv are smaller but they take ages to build on Windows because of autotools (if they build at all because again autotools), and they are also LGPL which may be important for commercial Qt customers.
I see your point. As a workaround, you can use private API:
bool qIsEffectiveTLD(QStringView domain)
is exported in Qt6Network (see
QtNetwork/private/qtldurl_p.h
), which you can arguably use to iterate over a QUrl.
There is no guarantee that this header or declarations is not changed in future Qt versions though. And keep in mind the limitations on validity of data ...

content.text: In case of QtNetwork the problem mostly occurs in error handling: a signal has a very generic name 'error', and then the getter (which returns the error that also was reported by the signal) has the same name. The safest approach is to rename the getter. Changing the signal's name would silently break the code that still would compile and later fail to report errors at run-time. For each class modified we'd have to update tests, documentation and examples. Classes in questions are:
QLocalSocket
QAbstractSocket
QNetworkReply
QSslSocket
Maybe we should do some reasearch on clazy and have it print a message if it identifies where qoverload is needed.
https://github.com/KDE/clazy/blob/master/docs/checks/README-overloaded-signal.md
Note that this check was added in 'master' - clazy 1.7 which is not released yet -> build clazy from src.

Timur mentioned: The name of the signal needs to stay the same and the getter must be changed (due to the old syntax where signal-existence was checked at runtime, changing signal name would silently break programs)
But this is Qt6, so we would be able to do this, after all.
Yes we want to keep breakages minimal, but if we see this as crucial enough, I do not see a reason to stop ourselves from doing so.
Except for people who compile with deprecated functionality removed, who will not notice anything.
Also, does the old signal syntax trigger deprecation warnings on usage? (hopefully?)
> Note that this check was added in 'master' - clazy 1.7 which is not released yet -> build clazy from src.

content.text: Some classes are using overloads for signals. While this was perfectly fine in a Qt 4 context and the old connect syntax, this forces to users to qOverloadOf connect statements due to ambiguity. This results in hard to read code and could be optimized by more explicit signatures.
The idea is not to remove qOverloadOf completely, rather to reduce the need for it in the API itself for Qt 6.

items.fromString: Improve signal signatures to be more explicit
items.toString: Improve signal signatures to avoid qOverloadOf in QtCore

items.fromString:
Some classes are using overloads for signals. While this was perfectly fine in a Qt 4 context and the old connect syntax, this forces to users to qOverloadOf connect statements due to ambiguity. This results in hard to read code and could be optimized by more explicit signatures.

 

The idea is not to remove qOverloadOf completely, rather to reduce the need for it in the API itself for Qt 6.
items.toString:
Some classes are using overloads for signals. While this was perfectly fine in a Qt 4 context and the old connect syntax, this forces to users to qOverloadOf connect statements due to ambiguity. This results in hard to read code and could be optimized by more explicit signatures.
In case of QtNetwork the problem mostly in error reporting: the signal has a very generic name 'error', and then the getter (returning the error
that also was reported by the signal) has the same name. The safest approach is to rename the getter. The opposite would silently break the code
that still would compile and fail to report errors at runtime. For each class modified we'd have to update tests, documentation and examples.
 

The idea is not to remove qOverloadOf completely, rather to reduce the need for it in the API itself for Qt 6.

content.text: We should try to connect even if some data points to us being disconnected (e.g. OS reporting LAN access only, or disconnected).

With both bearer (and now QNetworkStatusMonitor) there have been cases where making connections is impossible. These scenarios include being connected to VPN, where the OS thinks we're unable to access anything, or trying to connect when the OS is unable to ping their service of choice to see if it's accessible (done periodically, most commonly fails after reestablishing a connection or shortly after boot).
If we instead try to make the connection then it will still work reliably in these situations, and we'll just fail to connect if there's actually no network.
Note: it's not about removing QNetworkStatusMonitor (it has different thought-of usecases...), just about not using it to pre-emptively abort connections.

— Fix Version/s:

QNAM: Remove network connectivity pre-check (I37fc6905) · Gerrit Code Review (qt-project.org)

fields.summary: Add support for automatic unwrapping QFuture inside of .then()

issuetype.description: Public suggestions
issuetype.name: Suggestion

content.text: When creating a Async pipeline sometimes QFuture.then() may return QFuture. It's useful to unwrap the returned QFuture such there's not QFuture<QFuture<T>>. For example:
Things to consider when implementing unwrapped QFutures this:
Handling / propagating progress
Handling errors
Handling canceling and pausing
This is functionality is supported by the
AsyncFuture
library.
Looking forward to a solution
Unfortunately it's too late for adding support of automatic unwrapping QFuture inside
.then()
, since it will change the return type of
.then()
that used to return
QFuture<QFuture<T>
> and might cause SC breaks. Added
QFuture::unwrap()
instead, that can be used in the following way with the example in the description:

auto future = QtConcurrent::run(download, url)
            .then(processTiles)
            .unwrap()
            .then(saveImage)
unwrap()
returns a new future, that is fulfilled when the nested future is fulfilled, and it supports propagation of errors/cancelation. More detailed docs can be found
here

On imx6 this caused tearing artifacts because the decoder started writing a new frame to the same buffer, which could still be read from at this point.
the problem is the GPU rendering asynchronous and that it might not yet be done
while the GPU renders the current frame, the CPU is already preparing the next one and sometimes even more than one
he assumes that even the additional buffer that was introduced by this patch is sometimes given back to the decoder too early
DRM (GPU side) relies on a implicit sync at many stages, but
v4ldec
does not understand this
the decoder might already write the next frame to the buffer, while the GPU is still reading from it
there is a workaround for Gstreamer’s
qml6glsink
for this
the buffer to be returned is held for an additional frame in the sink until it is actually returned
this tells the pipeline how many buffers are required for the sink:
https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/gstreamer/gstreamer/-/blob/c086c83ac432879d01175f6ab0e05523f8b95f8e/subprojects/gst-plugins-good/ext/qt6/gstqml6glsink.cc#L527
the additional buffer hold is implemented here:
https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/gstreamer/gstreamer/-/blob/c086c83ac432879d01175f6ab0e05523f8b95f8e/subprojects/gst-plugins-good/ext/qt6/qt6glitem.cc#L343-L359
the "clear cut way to tell when the GPU is done" would be using a fence in the Qt rendering thread and communicating this back to the GStreamer thread
but this would have to be implemented differently for every API the Qt Rendering Hardware Interface supports and also needs to be wrapped in a GStreamer sync object
as this is not implemented (also not for the
qml6glsink
), the workaround would be to hold the buffer for another additional frame (i.e. also 2 frames like
qml6glsink
does) and cross your fingers that this is sufficient
the CPU will also be throttled and does not prepare more frames if the GPU can’t keep up, but this not guaranteed to happen after one frame
qml6glsink
is using a fence to ensure that all OpenGL operations are done before returning the buffer to Qt:
https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/gstreamer/gstreamer/-/blob/c086c83ac432879d01175f6ab0e05523f8b95f8e/subprojects/gst-plugins-good/ext/qt6/gstqml6glsink.cc#L535

setting QT_MULTIMEDIA_FORCE_GL_TEXTURE_EXTERNAL_OES is not necessary to use dmabuf. In my testing I've seen identical performance with the two options. See the updated commit message for details. Note that we're testing on Toradex Apalis iMX6, which is setup with i.MX 6 Quad.
