fields.summary: Improve the Android emulator CI workflow

issuetype.description: A user story for the product
issuetype.name: User Story

content.text: The current Android emulator keeps having issues from time to time. The common issue is the failure to launch the emulator properly each time on test VMs. We could try to fix this. We have two options that we could try out:
Make a snapshot of the avd during the provisioning and then when starting the test vms we could simply load back the snapshot and not do a full cold boot all over again
Add these flags to the avd launch comman
-no-window -no-boot-anim
Might be worth also looking into disabling
https://developer.android.com/studio/releases/emulator#file-backed-guest-RAM-snapshots
with QuickbootFileBacked = off. Using snapshots seems to disable it also, adding this as another benefit of them.

Helps if it can reduce I/O which is pretty bad on the VMs by not needlessly auto saving the AVD state as it will be disposed along with the VM anyways. We already use "-no-snapshot-load -no-snapshot-save", but I can't tell from docs that if those options do anything regards to the option.
Came across of it with the trace below from a VM, which seems to blow on some kind of paging or I/O
https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1931037
https://pastebin.com/raw/3kpjKHvL
wk22 refe:
Agreed to do. We could do both options and suggestion from

Added patches to move the emulator script from qtbase to qt5 to allow starting the emualtor easily during provisioning, and added option to create snapshot at that first start. atm there is still some issues getting that to work.
Here is a summary of what's been done under this story so far.
Generating a Snapshot
The speed advantage of using snapshots

Looking at some coin logs and from a debug VM, I did few emulator runs with various flags and it seems that having a snapshot ready during the start of each and every module test run would cut some good amount of time (~2 minutes) and also in general have the emulator in a ready state where no first time setup is being done in the background which can affect its performance. The time command is used for these results, and emulator_api_23_x86 AVD is used.
First time run:                                                  real: 2m8.694s,    user: 0m1.337s,  sys: 0m2.736s
Consecutive run without snapshot loading: real: 0m20.803s,  user: 0m0.167s,  sys: 0m0.349s
Consecutive run with snapshot loading:       real: 0m2.719s,    user: 0m0.034s, sys: 0m0.054s
From the stats above, a run with a ready snapshot is much faster and also would be much less flaky since the emulator would be in a ready state after all the initial setup and app loading is done.
Enabling Snapshot Use in COIN CI
In the patch
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/490490

, I try to run the emulator in a new mode during provisioning. Basically, the idea is to start the emulator using the existing script, and make sure that a snapshot is saved during that run (i.e. -no-snpashot-save flag is not used), and then wait a moment for the emulator to finish any initial setup jobs, then stop it which will make it save a snapshot to disk. In this case, the snapshot is called default_boot. And then do this for each emulator in CI during provisioning, so that in the test run we get a very fast emulator startup.
Unfortunately, that didn’t go as planned, most likely because of nested virtualization is not fully ready during the provisioning
Few things were attempting to tackle this issue
Use different -gpu flag

since in our CI we can’t use full hw acceleration from the host (i.e. -gpu host), we use swiftshader_indirect. However, for the provisioning step I tried to also use -gpu guest which actually worked for the Android 6 emulator and in few cases it was starting and generated a snapshot. But apparently, that has been disabled in the more recent Android versions like Android 12 and 13 that are in CI also. For those latter cases, the -gpu will be switched back to swiftshader_indirect, and the emulator just gets stuck for long time and don’t start.
Playing with KVM rules
In the thread
https://github.com/ReactiveCircus/android-emulator-runner/issues/46

there is discussion about starting the Android emulator in virtualized environments, which is similar to what we have. I tried to set the following rules for KVM but also didn’t work and didn’t help with starting the emulator.

echo 'KERNEL=="kvm", GROUP="kvm", MODE="0666", OPTIONS+="static_node=kvm"' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-kvm4all.rules
sudo udevadm control --reload-rules
sudo udevadm trigger --name-match=kvm
Putting the Android setup scripts at the end of the execution

the current Android scripts are numbered as 40-android_linux.sh and to make sure they are run at the very end when everything else has been set up already, they can be named as 99-android_linux.sh. However, that also didn’t help with starting the emulator during provisioning.
Next Step / Another Solution

can COIN restart the VM after provisioning and start the android emulator just after that (while still in provisioning)? So that whatever KVM/virtualization magic that’s done after the reboot is available for the emulator in provisioning?
Using Cached Snapshot Files in COIN CI

Since starting the emulator in provisioning didn’t work, the next option is to generate a snapshot manually and then cached its files and make them available during the Android setup to re-use them. That approach was done in
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/490489

. This one also had limitations, for some reason the extraction of the emulator files and snapshot were very slow, and even after that, the emulator start-up wasn’t as fast as shown in the stats above, were the average start was taking up to 50 seconds, which imo doesn’t justify all that manual work to prepare the snapshots.
Other Changes
After that, I went ahead with few improvements to the emulator scripts:
Moving the script to qt5 so that it’s closer to the Android setup scripts, and so that doing changes to it won’t need to wait for a submodule update to propagate to all other modules (
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/490486
Use -avd flag instead of direct name, this avoids the need to provide the name with a ‘@‘ prefix character and avoid some confusion sometimes.

Using -detect-image-hang -restart-when-stalled flags which can help the emulator recover from freezes, although these two flags are not that well documented on how exactly they work. This is output for the first flag for example:

ERROR: detected a hanging thread 'QEMU2 main loop'. No response for 15000 ms Process finished with 
exit code 139 (interrupted by signal 11: SIGSEGV)
Don’t ever use -no-snapshot-load since that serves up no good.
Use -no-window -no-boot-anim which can make the boot slightly faster and in any case we usually don’t need the emulator window to be shown and it can run headless.
Get rid of the nested virtualization warning dialog anyways with -no-nested-warnings.
Write the Android logcat logs to a file which can be examined afterwards in cases of failure or crashes, this is useful to examine logs that are not caught by Qt Test Lib such as System logs.

Make both logcat and emulator run logs available under the test results artifacts in COIN. This allows to check the logs without having to necessarily obtain a debug VM just to reproduce the failure and see the logs (handled in both
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/490487
and
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/490448
Yet Another Attempt to Improve the Android Emulator
In the patch
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/491459

is an attempt to run the emulator script as a background watcher, it would start the emulator and stay in the background to check if the adb shell is still responsive or not, and if not, it would kill the current “stuck” emulator instance and start it again. This would save us a lot of time, since many integrations in COIN fail because of the Android emulator becoming stuck and then the whole integration is stopped and re-run again which takes time and resources. So attempting to restart the emulator in the same integration seems like a good option to improve the overall emulator in CI state.
ATM, it seems that the COIN shell doesn’t want to let go of the emulator script and doesn’t want to disown it to let it run in the background to achieve this. This needs more investigation...
Cc:
Any ideas what’s needed to allow running a script in background in COIN?
Android Linux Setup Script Refactoring
In
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/490488

, is an improvement to the setup scripts which atm feels its a bit unorganized and changes like version bumps and emulator versions can be scattered around. So the patch does a re-organiztion and separate responsibilities into functions, so that any upcoming changes are very clear and require minimum changes.
Submodule update passed. Now, it seems that multi-abi test target was not explicitly setting an emulator name, and thus it fails to stage
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/490623
and this patch
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/493361
fixes that.
As for the detached background process, it might work by adding the following to the emulator command to overcome what appears to be a Go language bug:
</dev/null
<< Unfortunately, that didn’t go as planned, most likely because of nested virtualization is not fully ready during the provisioning
Hmm. What kind of problems the emulator startup caused?

<<can COIN restart the VM after provisioning and start the android emulator just after that (while still in provisioning)? So that whatever KVM/virtualization <<magic that’s done after the reboot is available for the emulator in provisioning?

VM will be restarted once after the provisioning to make sure that provisioning didn't break the VM. But I don't think you can run anything during that boot up at least through provisioning scripts. That would require some additional magic.
> Hmm. What kind of problems the emulator startup caused?
The emulator just gets stuck, nothing happens, as if it's frozen it fails to boot, and I'm assuming it has to do with hw acceleration, but it could be something else.
As for the rebooting, if we can have that or at least if there's a way to test it in the CI it would be worth a shot, is there anyway to achieve that?

There shouldn't be any difference between tier1 and tier2 HW acceleration. Or at least nothing I can think of. Have you tried with different VM? If it still failing I would take already existing Tier2 image and test your change on top of that.
I wouldn't start touching to rebooting at this point. Not even sure how easy it is to achieve that
YET ANOTHER ATTEMPT TO IMPROVE THE ANDROID EMULATOR
In the patch
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/491459

is an attempt to run the emulator script as a background watcher, it would start the emulator and stay in the background to check if the adb shell is still responsive or not, and if not, it would kill the current “stuck” emulator instance and start it again. This would save us a lot of time, since many integrations in COIN fail because of the Android emulator becoming stuck and then the whole integration is stopped and re-run again which takes time and resources. So attempting to restart the emulator in the same integration seems like a good option to improve the overall emulator in CI state.
ATM, it seems that the COIN shell doesn’t want to let go of the emulator script and doesn’t want to disown it to let it run in the background to achieve this. This needs more investigation...
Cc:
Any ideas what’s needed to allow running a script in background in COIN?
Maybe the stdin stdout stderr need to be redirected? I would run the "watcher" as a script separate from the launcher, directly launched as a Coin instruction, that would call a shell line like this:
sh -c "nohup emulator_watcher.sh &"

nohup does the redirection I talked about. Additionally, I wrapped it in "sh -c" because I assumed that Coin's ExecuteInstruction doesn't sub-execute a shell. If it does, then there is no need for that.
But how will this help? If the emulator gets stuck, it means that most likely some test is also stuck. Re-launching the emulator will not save the test.
Do we have some instance of stuck emulator in a VM somewhere? I could have a look, trying to figure out the reason it gets stuck.
thanks for the suggestion.

The theory that the emulator is getting stuck was my theory initially, but after part of this work that allowed to get hold of the emulator logcat, it seems that the emulator wasn't really getting stuck because there were logcat logs after that freeze timestamp and during all the duration before it's killed (15 mins). So, it seems that the test was getting stuck or the test runner or maybe something else (??)

So I think at this point, trying to add a script to use nohup to restart the daemon might not be all that much valuable, especially, that the reason it still might happen again and the test freezes or it would not happen again (flaky) and would get unnoticed if we simply restart the emulator.
Agreed, lets skip the emulator restart, I don't think it's needed any longer!

So I'm closing this now, as the main reason this work was done was to avoid the frequent random emulator freezes, but after part of the work done here (for example making the logcat of each integration available to download) and some other work done to improve the androidtestrunner. It seems that the theory that all those freezes are cause by the emulator image or virtualization is not entirely true, as many case I've manually checked it seems that the emulator seemed stuck but it was actually the test being stuck and cmake was passing --timeout -1 argument to androidtestrunner which means it was waiting forever. That behavior was improved in QTBUG-106479 and now androidtestrunner takes the cmake timeout.

So the conclusion of this is that the emulator freezes indicate a test issue and the offending test (usually the last test before the freeze) is the reason and that should be fixed or handled in some other way instead. And of course that means also trying to restart the emulator wouldn't yield any better outcome as far as the offending test will be executed again the emulator might freeze again anyway.

content.text: As a developer, I want to register Qt installations on my development
machine. One of the Qt versions is marked as the default one.
These registered Qt installations are then used for building Qt projects and running Qt-specific tools.
It would be cool if it was possible to have a configuration value with Qt version names as enum items. However, that doesn't seem possible at the moment. Upstream feature request:
https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/187141
The VSCode cmake extension has Kit autodetection built-in. Maybe we can contribute code to extend theirs?
A CMake kit in VS Code represents a locally installed toolchain. I have for instance gcc, clang and gcc/mingw.
Combining this with Qt installations we would have Qt installation x compatible toolchain.
In my case I'd have two kits per desktop Qt installation. That feels a bit... convoluted.
Or you'd add one kit per Qt installation + standard compiler.
What's the standard compiler in my case? gcc or clang?
On Linux ? c++ / g++ / clang++ (in that order)
On Mac ? clang
On Windows ? msvc if its there
The location for auto-detect is OS-dependent:
Windows
%APPDATA%\Code\User\settings.json
macOS
~/Library/Application Support/Code/User/settings.json
Linux
~/.config/Code/User/settings.json
"vscode-qt-tools.qtInstallations": [ ... ]
may be written by Qt maintenance tool.{{{}{}}}
The path may change if the user has profiles enabled, mine for instance is:
~/Library/Application Support/Code/User/profiles/-7824a8e6/settings.json
I guess that
is right in
https://qt-project.atlassian.net/browse/VSCODEEXT-4?focusedCommentId=2027187&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels:comment-tabpanel
that someone should contribute to CMake's Qt installation detection.
CMake has no Qt (working) installation detection. And it should not have one. There already are established ways to find Qt packages with CMake.

What Marcus suggested was to extend VS Code's CMake Tools extension to add Qt support to it. This is also flawed. I'm 100 % sure that upstream will reject such attempts to add support for a - from their point of view - random library to their toolchain detection code.
Would the upstream consider accepting detection of the CMake distribution installed with Qt?
Would the upstream consider accepting detection of the CMake distribution installed with Qt?

I don't see any detection code other than "use the cmake executable reachable from PATH". People can configure the location of CMake. An addition to the CMake Tools extension that detects the CMake distribution that comes with Qt is most probably a hard sell.
Regarding how to locate all the Qt installations present on a system, there is no global registry etc. maintained by the Qt (Online) Installer.
When using the Qt (Online) Installers each Qt package will register itself as a Kit for QtCreator:
/home/<user>/Qt6x/Tools/QtCreator/share/qtcreator/QtProject/qtcreator/qtversion.xml
But the user may install multiple QtSDKs on a system and the QtSDK installation path can be pretty much anything.
Thanks
I found `%appdata%\QtProject\qtcreator\qtversion.xml` on Windows.
I guess we can use this file.
Please, consider creating something compatible to QtCreator installation optionability.
Meanwhile we must have a workaround for this yet potential situation.
%appdata%\QtProject\qtcreator\qtversion.xml
is not the same as
/home/<user>/Qt6x/Tools/QtCreator/share/qtcreator/QtProject/qtcreator/qtversion.xml
%appdata%\QtProject\qtcreator\qtversion.xml  only contains Qt Versions that were manually added by the user.

As Iikka said, there is no way right now to find Qt Installation folders (though I think there should be). You could try to guess the default installation location, on macOS that would be ~/Qt, not sure on windows, but you will need to allow the user to choose an installation folder and then check <installation-folder>/Tools/sdktool/QtProject/qtcreator/qtversion.xml yourself.
Thank you
on you really valuable note here. It appears to be that Start Menu launchers currently is the only reliable place to get Qt installation path automatically for Windows.
, JFYI, until QtCreator launched that file is not created, I double checked this Marcus's suggestion.
Anyway, Start Menu lnks work for Windows just fine.
Setting aside the case of custom builds, which may or may not have been "properly installed", should we also consider other likely scenarios of Qt installation, like vcpkg or conan?

Other likely installation scenarios can be considered but maybe in separate issues. I expect the extension's behavior to be different if you use vcpkg's manifest mode for instance where you have the Qt installation under the project's build root.
Hi
, I confirm that the qtversion.xml is not created until QtCreator first run
suggests to add qtpath-based detector too:
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt-labs/vscodeext/+/517384/comments/c206a28b_8596f951
`qtpath -query QT_INSTALL_BINS`
Considered done.

fields.summary: Lock Active Workspace

issuetype.description: Public suggestions
issuetype.name: Suggestion

customfield_10020.name: QDS Berlin - 2023 Week 43/44
customfield_10020.goal: Feature freeze in the next sprint (first half-mid of November)

content.text: As a user, I wish to lock the active Workspace.
By locking the active Workspace, all Views will remain in their current placement within the active Workspace.
When the active Workspace is locked, a user will no longer be able to move/place the Views via drag and drop (which brings up the blue placement boxes).

When the active Workspace is locked, a user will no longer be able to add or subtract Views via the Menu Bar drop down until the active Workspace is unlocked. Suggest that the menu is grayed out when active Workspace is locked.
When the active Workspace is locked, a user can still resize windows by dragging them from the edge of any window.  However each View window itself will remain attached to it's fixed location.
Once a user unlocks the active Workspace, the user will be able to alter Workspace normally.
The user's selection of locked vs unlocked will remain constant and saved.
If a user quits Design Studio, the user's previous selection for Locked vs Unlocked Workspace will remain.
is this possible with ADS?
Needs to be tested. There is this configuration
dockwidgetmovable
, but I don't know if it does what the user really wants.
Thanks for looking into this Henning.  Let me know if you need anything tested.
any progress here?  Thank you.
ToolTip changed to "Sets the visible Views to immovable across the Workspaces."

content.text: The task is to update provisioning scripts to build FFmpeg with the --enable-shared and the
--disable-static flag on platforms where this is possible.
The FFmpeg backend must be updated to use dynamic linking to FFmpeg.
The discussion page:
https://intranet.qt.io/display/QTRD/Shipping+of+shared+FFmpeg+with+dependencies
Duplicating the discussion page here:
We're working on replacing static FFmpeg linkage with a dynamic one to comply with the LGPL license.
On the platforms where FFmpeg depends only on system libraries (Windows, macOS), everything goes smoothly: we install FFmpeg shared libs together with qt libraries.
On Linux and Android, to implement the dynamic linkage, we need to sort out FFmpeg extra dependencies:
OpenSSL (Linux, Android) - need for playing for secure network streams
VAAPI (Linux) - hw accelerated decoding/encoding.
In the future, we might add Vulkan, VDPAU, etc...
Dependencies:
Now the problem with dependencies is resolved via stubs.
'Stub' implies that we do the job instead of the dynamical Unix linker:
we load the libraries manually (QLibrary::load which does dlopen),
find symbols there (QLibrary::resolve which does dlsym).

Some thoughts of security regarding public symbols in stubs.
As QtMultimedia loads the FFmpeg plugin via dlopen+RTLD_LOCAL, the global symbols scope is not polluted.
If a user leverages own OpenSSL or VAAPI on their side, the FFmpeg libraries can catch symbols with the same name + version (optional) from the global scope instead of the stub library.

The libraries expose the following symbols: OpenSSL 1.x.x - non-versioned symbols; OpenSSL 3.x.x - symbols with API version 3.0.0 (we're using it); VAAPI - non-versioned symbols apart vaCreateSurface, it has vaCreateSurface@0.33 (main) and vaCreateSurface@0.32 - for backward compatibility. Non-versioned symbols in VAAPI are binary compatible in different versions.
We check in cmake and will declare in the documentation that VAAPI 0.32 ABI is not supported (it's 11 years old), so only vaCreateSurface@0.33 is exposed by the stub.
Considering the previous 2 points, the FFmpeg libs can catch binary compatible symbols from the global scope, which is not supposed to be a security issue.
Considering having a stubs managing script, we will document that we recommend switching to the original dependency if using own VAAPI or OpenSSL.

Based on some discussion and thinking, I think of all the options presented here, option 2 is both the most elegant and scalable for all cases where FFmpeg itself can gracefully fail if a dependency isn't present. It avoids that we have to maintain patches on top of FFmpeg sources or build system, and gives us a reliable and graceful way to degrade.

The question is then what the defaults should be. Thiago's idea of shipping two sets of plugins seems heavy-handed, given that it'd be trivial to turn the one set into the other set with the help of a

script. Can we expect that users installing Qt as an SDK on their development host can also install all required dependencies expected by our FFmpeg binary? It's already hard to get a development environment set up, and we definitely don't want to distribute OpenSSL etc as shared libraries as part of a Qt installation just to get the FFmpeg backend to work. And even if that is realistic, can we then expect such users to patch the libraries as part of packaging the redistributables so that their application works (possibly with degraded functionality) on a system where not all dependencies are present?
If so, then us shipping a set of plugins and FFmpeg libraries that doesn't use stubs would at least work.

But that's a big "IF", and I don't quite see the benefit over defaulting to a patched library that goes through the stubs and works on any system, with or without e.g. VAAPI. If we were to sign our binaries (and I'm not sure if we do; don't think so), then we would do so after patching. And users cannot really expect a set of binaries from any other source to have the same signature as what we ship. And if they remove the stubs, then they would have to sign the binaries themselves again anyway.

I repeat: modifying shipped files should be a last resort. Please find a solution that does not create a file that gets loaded into memory but can't be cryptographically signed by whoever compiled it. I don't think the Qt Company signs the binaries today, but it should be an option.
Also, for security reasons, don't ship plugins without all their dependencies being present. The deployment scripts need to verify that.

libavcodec58 means /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libavcodec.so.58
libavcodec60 means /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libavcodec.so.60
libavcodec61 means /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libavcodec.so.61
And handbrake links to libavcodec58 instead of libavcodec, then it's not difficult to have multiple versions of libavcodec together.
But for the PPA ubuntuhandbook1/ffmpeg6 and ubuntuhandbook1/ffmpeg7, it tries to upgrade or only keeps one version, which is not very convenient.
For Ubuntu 24.04(LTS, noble), it should have ffmpeg 6.1.1(libavcodec60)
https://launchpad.net/ubuntu/noble/+package/ffmpeg
https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble/libavcodec60

If you want to ship a patched set of FFmpeg libraries such that they are loadable if OpenSSL or VAAPI are absent but use them if they are present, that's your prerogative. That's a good thing and maybe you should consider upstreaming the change, with a configure-time option to ffmpeg. And of course, what you build, you should be able to sign.

I think that having graceful degradation and hard failures in the same set of libraries is too much to ask for. They should just install another set of ffmpeg libraries instead. Whether TQtC is also providing those is yet another question. But PLEASE don't create it by having the users do binary-paching on the set of libraries from the previous paragraph. Assume that any binary that you produce and is downloadable from download.qt.io is immutable.

Given the above, then I agree that dlopening the libraries helps little: the plugin is unusable and therefore useless. However, as Liang has just pointed out, the ffmpeg libraries change SONAME very frequently. So dlopening them MAY allow supporting multiple different versions from the plugin without recompilation, and thus allow using the distribution-provided ffmpeg library set. It solves a
different
problem.

Agree that we don't need to give users a "patch our binary" solution if they instead can build FFmpeg themselves, get it from some upstream source, or have in general no disadvantage from using our stubs.
Also agree that upstreaming patches to FFmpeg to dlopen libssl or VAAPI might be a good thing to do in parallel.
And
if

we can support multiple versions of FFmpeg, then dlopening them might be an idea for the future; it'll be a fair bit of work, which is wasted if libraries with a changed SONAME change behavior frequently enough to break our code anyway.
The solution is ready:
In QtMM:
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtmultimedia/+/552196
and the relation chain
In Qt/qt5:
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/550318
Doesn't seem to have taken into consideration any of the recent discussion. I've stated my advice (which you asked for).
, I've taken into consideration your advice to avoid patching binaries on the user side. Now users can replace the shipped ffmpeg with their one without any patching.
Ok, I will reread the patches. Please note the qtmultimedia one contains changes related to OpenSSL, so I will not be able to leave a comment there.
And by that I mean that you have a -1 but I can't tell you what it is.

content.text: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_Adaptive_Streaming_over_HTTP
ffmpeg (or at least ffplay) can play these streams, but they don't work in Qt multimedia.
Example stream:
https://livesim.dashif.org/livesim/chunkdur_1/ato_7/testpic4_8s/Manifest.mpd
See also
The structure of an MPEG-DASH MPD - Brendan Long
Task for sprint 23-24: Check if DASH streams work out of the box if FFmpeg is built with libxml support.
> Check if DASH streams work out of the box if FFmpeg is built with libxml support.
I believe that might indeed solve the issue. But please consider testing it with one of these streams instead
http://ftp.itec.aau.at/datasets/DASHDataset2014/BigBuckBunny/10sec/
I was able to make DASH streams work but with some caveats.
In order to enable DASH streams FFmpeg should be configured with
--enable-libxml2
. There is also a switch
--enable-demuxer=dash

but I was able to make it work with and without it, probably it is enabled by default or automatically if libxml2 is specified (need to verify). Made it work on MacOS, still struggling to make it work on Windows/MSYS, libxml-2.0 is not found by pkg-config. Additional path-related configuration is required because libxml headers are not found during FFmpeg configuration (my investigation stopped here for now). For MacOS did some similar stuff since the same problem has occurred:

export LDFLAGS="-L$(brew --prefix libxml2)/lib"
export CPPFLAGS="-I$(brew --prefix libxml2)/include"
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="-$(brew --prefix libxml2)/lib/pkgconfig"
Unfortunately that didn't make it work  right away. The problem was with
avformat_open_input
. Currently we pass
nullptr
as third argument, which is format and the function fails. If I manually create format and pass it then it works (kinda).
auto format = av_find_input_format("dash");

However, the quality of the resulting stream is of very poor quality even though when played via ffplay the quality is good. Worth mentioning that I've built ffplay as part of FFmpeg build, so everything in terms of configuration is the same. My assumption is that input stream of the lowest quality is selected. Need further investigation on how to do it properly.
For testing purposes I uses the requested stream -
http://ftp.itec.aau.at/datasets/DASHDataset2014/BigBuckBunny/10sec/
One more thing, if I build FFmpeg (and subsequently ffplay) without libxml then DASH streams do not work even via ffplay. Therefore
--enable-libxml2
is definitely required to make it work.
Thank you for investigating
. It looks like vcpkg struggles with a similar issue. See
vcpkg/ports/ffmpeg/0015-Fix-xml2-detection.patch at 2024.05.24 · microsoft/vcpkg (github.com)
. This was later changed in [[alsa,fdk-aac,ffmpeg,libsrt,snappy,x265] Code cleanup, fix and use pk… · microsoft/vcpkg@2017886 (github.com)|
https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg/commit/2017886818a9a88d303548b53709f5ef922efb39
If patching the configure script solves the problem, we could consider doing the same in one of the upcoming sprints.
Yes, patching the configure script seems like the only option now. I've tried it after I posted my previous comment and eventually I've got to the linker error that
xml2.lib
was missing. I'm still looking into possible solutions but currently I do not have any. Need to study your links more closely maybe there's a solution.

content.text: Based on:
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/558271
"unsupported android version", given that from 6.8 onwards that will be Android 9 and it is not possible to build for older versions like Android 8 after that change.
As suggestion:

Add a configure flag to enable building Qt for older Android OS versions (which might still work even if not supported) in order to bypass the hardcoded limitation for those users who want to build Qt for older versions of Android.
Or add to the Qt for Android documentation that compiling against versions older than <x> is not supported but might work and revert the:
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/558271
I think this cannot be done, especially from the "support promise" perspective. Anyway I leave this to you since, it's something that I cannot evaluate the need of.
I think this goes against support promise indeed, if we add such flag it might imply that it's supported to build for older versions, while it's not. The page
https://doc-snapshots.qt.io/qt6-dev/android-supported-versions-selection-guidelines.html#minimum-supported-version

already mentions that it might work if you do your own build with build system changes, however, adding Gerrit patches is not usually done for our docs, it can get outdated very quick and be obsolete. And for Qt 6.8 now I think this ticket would serve that purpose of closing the gap for people needing to revert to older versions by reverting

content.text: Following C++ API review rounds, and because of the QML embedding into native Android apps, the Java APIs, will be more exposed to users. Thus, to keep changes in check, do steps to start a formal API review round for Java.
This would ideally mean having a script(s) that makes the process automated, that would eventually live under qtqa/scripts/api-review.

I've looked into javap and javadoc tools for generating public API changes that can then be used to generate a diff. javadoc seems more promising because it would include the actual docs changes and not only the high level declarations that's generated with javap. Using javadoc Doclet API it might be possible to create a custom format like Markdown instead of the default HTML format.
I have been looking into
javadoc
using a custom
Doclet
to generate markdown which might look simpler and easier to make a diff of including the docs. That approach looks more promising than using
javap
. I'm using a fork of a library I found that achieves that, and I've been adding changes on top of it to tailor it for my needs
https://github.com/Issam-b/markdowndoclet

The main issue so far is with Gerrit changes, since the diff is done on this generated (pseudo) code, I'm forced to make two commits, one as a base containing the previous version API and the actual API review diff on top of it containing the new API. The only option I see is to commit the generated API text for each Qt version so doing the diff in the next version would be easy.
The current implementation for the script works for bash and zsh. Most of the comments are addressed as well, waiting now for another round of review.
As a side note, the Doctlet code is still needing some cleanup, and will do that separately, esp. that now we have plans to use it to generate Java API docs for our docs with qdoc.

fields.summary: Investigate reason for cut sound with QSoundEffect on Windows

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done
issuetype.name: Task

customfield_10020.goal: Get started on OKR tasks, fix high priority bugs

content.text: The qml-minimal-sound-effect manual test plays a sound that should have two distinct peaks, like two drops hitting the water. When played on Windows, only one is heard, even with environment variable QT_DISABLE_AUDIO_PREPARE=0

Note that when adding a Sleep(500) before releasing the m_audioClient in QWindowsAudioSink::close() fixes the problem, even with QT_DISABLE_AUDIO_PREPARE=1. This might indicate that the IAudioClient interface is released before it is finished playing.
See sequence diagram for the setup of QSoundEffect with the qml-minimal-sound-effect manual test, where releasing the IAudioClient interface happens at the very bottom.

If we do not release the m_renderClient in QWindowsAudioSink::close(), the sound is no longer cut, and everything appears to work fine. It could be useful to change the design of the QWindowsAudioClient such that the IAudioClient and IAudioRenderClient instances were created when constructing the QWindowsAudioSink, and not released until the QWindowsAudioSink is destroyed. This may prevent changing buffer size on the fly.
See also:
Windows-universal-samples/Samples/WindowsAudioSession/cpp/WASAPIRenderer.cpp at 534d40ae64cc6a0ad03b1f0c53236845125abeb2 · microsoft/Windows-universal-samples

content.text: Historically, Android has only supported 4 KB memory page sizes, which has optimized system memory performance for the average amount of total memory that Android devices have typically had. Beginning with Android 15, AOSP supports devices that are configured to use a page size of 16 KB (16 KB devices).
Qt for Android should be validated to work with such devices, i.e. it should be ensured that no hard-coded page sizes are used.
https://developer.android.com/guide/practices/page-sizes
You've created this as a task, not a bug or a suggestion. Have you talked to any developer that will do this work?
It's definitely not going to be me. I need to reassign this task.
Sorry I didn’t assign anyone specifically. "Task" just seemed like the most appropriate to me, but feel free to change as seen fit.
Do you have any evidence of a problem supporting those systems?
We had some internal talk to look at this, not many devices are available that fully support this though so I'm making it a P3
https://developer.android.com/guide/practices/page-sizes#developer-option
FYI, devices with 16 KB page size do crash with the current qt builds. See
. It's easy to reproduce using the recently-added 16 KB page size  emulators.
Google also provides a script
check_elf_alignment.sh
for checking alignment in the apk that could be useful in your CI (
https://developer.android.com/guide/practices/page-sizes#alignment-use-script
Google will require working 16kb Page size support by November 1 for Play Store, see also their blog post:
https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2025/05/prepare-play-apps-for-devices-with-16kb-page-size.html:
Starting November 1st, 2025, all new apps and updates to existing apps submitted to Google Play and targeting Android 15+ devices must support 16 KB page sizes.

fields.summary: It would be nice if we Enable consistent and enforceable OpenSSL deployment for Android in Qt

issuetype.description: Public suggestions
issuetype.name: Suggestion

content.text: In Qt Android projects, OpenSSL is required for HTTPS functionality (
QSslSocket
QNetworkAccessManager
WebEngine
, etc.). However, Qt does not provide a reliable, team-friendly way to enforce or manage OpenSSL deployment:
The mechanism in Qt Creator to include "SSL” generates a
.pri
file with hard-coded, machine-specific paths — not suitable for version control or CI.
Missing SSL causes silent runtime failures (e.g.,
supportsSsl()
returns false) with no build-time warnings or errors.
There is no standard
QT += openssl
Kind of mechanism or CMake equivalent to enforce presence and deployment of OpenSSL libraries.
It would be very nice if  we can have some kind of
qmake/CMake helper
QT += openssl
or
find_package(Qt6 REQUIRED COMPONENTS OpenSSL)
) that:
Fails configuration if OpenSSL is not found
Automatically adds
libssl.so
and
libcrypto.so
to
androiddeployqt
via
ANDROID_EXTRA_LIBS
or CMake equivalents
cc
Is the customer not happy with the instructions in
https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/android-openssl-support.html
? That is the best that we have atm. If there is something to improve, please specify by referring to documentation what sections and perhaps how (suggestions of the content) can be improved

Hi Rami. There must be an enforceable check at build time for OpenSSL. We do not need to ship it with the package, but projects built with OpenSSL shouldn't be able to build without actually having it available.

I work on a Qt-based developer SDK that connects to HTTPS services in most common use cases. On all platforms we support, except for Android, there is a default system TLS plugin that is always available, making it seamless for our users. However, on Android, Qt relies on OpenSSL, and there is no fallback option.

This situation means that while our users can configure their apps and run them on Android, they will encounter issues that lead to unexpected behavior. For instance, the app will run but display an empty screen, with no clear indication of the underlying problem—only a series of TLS warnings in the console that they might not notice. We do document that SSL is required, as you have done, but users still face this challenge.

To improve the user experience, we would like a way to indicate that SSL is required for certain apps when configuring with qmake or cmake, and the configure step should fail if it is not. Our goal is to provide our users with effective tooling and workflows, helping them avoid this common pitfall and reducing confusion about potential issues.

. With that you can keep OpenSSL in your find_package() and it would fail, but once you start using the OpenSSL from there (or build it yourself through the build script

The policies and documentation in
https://github.com/android/ndk/wiki#release-schedule
and release history; every 2
nd

release as LTS from 21 to 25, then LTS after LTS from 25, 26 and 27 and now suddenly skipping two releases 28 and 29 to be LTS's. And perhaps extending the LTS support of 27 from end of July 2025 to until NDK 30 comes out?

fields.summary: Investigate virtual camera options for Windows

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done
issuetype.name: Task

content.text: Investigate which command-line virtual camera options we have on windows OS.
In a nutshell:
It must be a command-line tool
Resolution, output stream, pixel formats, fps should be customizable.
Ideally, the option should be available on x86_64 and arm
check software licenses.
More info is in epic
https://qt-project.atlassian.net/browse/QTBUG-139771
The ticket includes:
find suitable software
make sure that it works locally
create a proof-of-concept script that installs the software (downloading, [opt] configuring+compiling, installing)
write investigation reports in the task comments.
The chosen approach is implementing minimal vcam code through windows API.
Some breakdowns.
- The vcam project has nothing to do with the qt framework, and it should stay separately.
- we want to be able to modify the vcam code and update the camera binaries on provisioning.
- the vcam project is compilable by msvc. The output is one or 2 exacutables + dll.

- the installation of the vcam binaries is supposed to be done by a provisioning script. Installation includes moving binaries to a proper place, adding a windows registry key, and setting an environment variable.
- in light of the installation point above, having vcam as a submodule doesn’t work for us.
- most likely, the vcam binaries are to be integrated only on windows 11 (some API is not available on windows 10).
Let’s look at potential solutions.
1. A provisioning script downloads sources, compiles, and installs binaries.
Note, that in this case, the provisioning script must refer to the exact commit sha; referring to the top of the branch can easily break provisioning without a breaking commit.
The qt5 provisioning compiles the binaries on every run. The vcam project is small, the expected compilation time is a few seconds.
Pros:
- a straight-forward implementation of the flow. Considering active development state of the vcam project, it’s a good option to maintain it.
- the solution is optimizable via advanced caching (
solution 4).
Cons:
- we’re adding +1 project that we compile on CI, which is not designed for compilation. Note, we already compile on CI different stuff (openssl, ffmpeg, flite, patchelf on some Linux’es)
2. Manually compile binaries and upload to ci-files.
Cons:
- hard to maintain. It’s easy to mix up versions by uploading something wrong.
3. Move the vcam project build system outside provisioning, to a specific repo outside qt5/ (e.g. qt_vcam), with its own continuous integration flow.
It’s 2 sub-options:
3.1. Sources are on gitlab, and the building flow is triggered by a new gitlab commit.
3.2. All sources are in the new repo, and we commit to it, and it’s triggered by the repo change.
In both cases, 3.1 and 3.2, the sources get compiled in the qt_vacam repo’s CI infrastructure, saved to
ci-files
with an accessible link, and get downloaded and installed by the provisioning script. Also, in theory, finishing building qt_vcam can trigger windows provisioning rebuild for consistency.
Pros:
- The sources are compiled only after the commit in vcam project
- no extra compilations in qt5 provisioning
Cons:
- efforts to create and maintain qt_vcam repo
- qt5 provisioning script has to download binaries without checksum verification (otherwise, we should sync the checksum every time, which is problematic).

- if CI for qt_vcam utilises installed qt5’s provisioning environment, it’s a cyclic dependency: qt_vcam refers to qt5’s provisioning, that contains the scripts “install-vcam.ps1“, that refers to build artifacts of qt_vcam.
4. On top of the solution 1: implement an advanced caching mechanism via a custom server.
The solution was presented on weekly demo around one year ago (unfortunately, the recorded video has been already deleted)
The idea is building any stuff, including vcam code on CI, but doing it only when any of it’s dependencies (e.g. the file install-vcam.ps1, msvc version) get changed.

In a nutshell, we run a custom http server that can save and return any binaries by some complex id, that represents the hash sum of the dependencies, version, type of product, etc, then the provisioning script wrappers check if the binaries are available for the current version/product/hashsum, then downloads them, or compiles and uploads. That said, recompiling of the binaries is only triggered by modifying the dependencies.
Links:
Custom server
caching machinery for shell scripts and its usage for building FFmpeg (actually, it’s the most complicated case)
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/602362
Pros:
- the approach considers distinguishing binaries by product, OS, version, and it’s reusable for other compilations in qt5 provisioning.
- we end up with compilation frequency similar to the
solution 3
Cons:
- a custom server requires any additional place to store it’s code (probably gitlab)
- a custom server may require extra maintanence (even though frequent cleanups/updates are not expected).
- additional wrapping scripting code in provisioning, for shell and ps1 scripts.
According to the latest discussion with
, we’re likely to go with the solution 1 since it’s the most straight-forward way to run vcam project and maintain it the first time. TBD
5. On top of solution 3 (separate
qtvcam
repo)
in qtmultimedia repo’s
dependencies.yaml
file add a dependency to qtvcam repo with the specific git SHA you want.
Do not involve provisioning at all.
Coin builds when needed, and transfers the artifacts automatically (like it does for all other dependencies).
Disadvantages:
Coin transfers the artifacts where it wants (IIRC under $HOME/qt/work). If we want custom installation path, Coin might need to be patched or other workaround applied.
Option 2 could be implemented in QtSdk like e.g.
https://qt-pkg.ci.qt.io/view/CI%20Network%20test/job/CI_Network_Tester/
Our coin download tools support (and encourage) SHA1 verification. Uploading wrong binaries can be excluded.
Option 2 means manual upload. You’re probably talking about solution 3

note, that vcam binaries should be installed for proper usage: the binaries have a dll, that is not used by qt; instead, it’s should be written to the windows registry so that it can be pulled by the operating system in proper time.
A change related to this issue (sha1 '2450189a4f52c48e7dcc174fd9ae4282b6c78e62')  was integrated in 'qt/qt5' in the 'dev' branch.
The task is solved. For now, installation is fixed with solution 1( a provisioning script downloads sources, compiles, and installs binaries).

issuetype.description: A task that needs to be done

content.text: There's an
enum.mustache
template file in the OpenAPI generator templates. The generated Enum class can be a base class for the model.
The templates also have
{{{}#isEnum
}} switch which is used in various places.
The only relevant part in the spec that I could find after a quick check is
https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.1.html#fixed-fields-4
, but I can be missing something.
The scope of this task is to check if the current implementation matches the OpenAPI spec and provide tests for the Enum objects.
I found a related open bugreport:
https://github.com/OpenAPITools/openapi-generator/issues/2645
It seems that the openapi generator handles the enums only when they are represented as separate schemas.
I tired to modify the

A change fixing this issue has been merged. Closing it automatically.

fields.summary: Allow using translations/localization in Android service process

issuetype.description: A user story for the product
issuetype.name: User Story

content.text: It seems that QLocale::system() and therefore also QLocale() don't return the configured system locale under Android when invoked from the service process. This in turn leads to translations not working there.

I therefore tried passing QLocale().bcp47Name() from the frontend to the service manually where I then invoked QLocale::setDefault(QLocale(passedBcp47Name)). The last invocation was in my tests effectively QLocale::setDefault(QLocale(QStringLiteral("de"))). This also didn't work because QLocale() still got me the "C" locale and translations were not working.
I therefore tried instantiating a QGuiApplication in the service process with the help of a previous change of my which got merged:
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/653832
Only with this setting it was possible to set the default locale in the service process manually.
With this I got translations working but this approach has some serious drawbacks:
It shouldn't be required to pass the locale from the frontend to the service manually.
It shouldn't be required to instantiate a QGuiApplication in the service process for localization to work. (QAndroidService should be enough.)
Instantiating a QGuiApplication didn't even work in all my tests.
It worked well with my x86-64 development build of Qt (with qtbase at
) in the emulator and Android 15.

It didn't work with my aarch64 release build of Qt (version 6.9.2) on a real Samsung phone with Android 14 because the service got stuck up on the QGuiApplication instantiation leading to Android producing an ANR for the service process. Not sure why that is. When I tested
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/653832
with Android 6.9.1 (or was it even still 6.9.0?) the icon rendering I used it for worked on the very same phone where it now gets stuck.

So if using a QGuiApplication is supposed to be "the way" despite 1 and 2 then 3.2 needs to be sorted out. (For the sake of doing image processing/rendering it would also generally make sense to sort this out - but that's a different feature request.) Maybe it only didn't work on the real phone because my aarch64 build is still based on Qt 6.9.2 and the problem is already fixed on the dev branch as of the mentioned commit.
Note that my use case for this is updating an Android notification from the service process even if the activity process isn't running.
I'm guessing (not really familiar with the Android architecture) your service is like a Unix dæmon, that user-space apps can talk to.
Does the Service run as a different user than the user app ?
Is "the activity" what I would think of as a user app ?

In so far as that's a decent model of what's happening, I can imagine the Android O/S layer may treat the service as user-neutral and thus run it in a "vanilla" environment, with no user-specific customisations, thus in particular no localisation.  That would be consistent with it getting the C locale by default, independent of the user's settings.  However, since an Android is generally a personal device, there may be some configuration option – maybe in the packaging or the manifest of the service – that would change that default so that it does get the user environment.  Unfortunately, being ignorant of Android, I can only guess at that, but maybe a colleague with better knowledge can help you with it, or you can find it yourself.
I'm also wondering
Why does the service need to do translations ?

For example, if it's generating messages for the user-facing app to display, surely it could deliver the messages in a locale-neutral way and leave the app to do the translation ?  If services are meant to be user-neutral, surely that's better than complicating the service with hooks to get it to adapt itself to match the user locale.
I certainly wouldn't expect to need a
QGuiApplication
in a non-graphical application, although a
QCoreApplication
may well be required to get
QTranslator
working, and
QGuiApplication
is based on
QCoreApplication
, so perhaps what made it work for you was actually something in the base class.
You should be able, even without (or before you create) a
Q*Application
, to create a
QLocale
from its constructors taking some combination of language, script and territory, or taking a string identifying a locale (such as
"de"
"de-Latn-DE"
or
"de-DE"
) and pass it to
QLocale::setDefault()
, although this only controls the process's default
QLocale
, not its system locale.  That should suffice to control what translations it uses, at least, although
QTranslator
may need
QCoreApplication
However, you seem to have tried that without success, leaving you still with the "C" locale.
Are you sure you asked for
QLocale()
, default-constructed, not
QLocale::system()
, which isn't affected by
QLocale::setDefault()
It's possible instantiating
QCoreApplication
is possible where
QGuiApplication
might present problems.  I'm not sure if it's needed for
QTranslator
to work, but it may indeed be needed.

However, coaxing the service into setting what it needs to use the user locale instead of the "vanilla" one is surely a work-around: the underlying problem is that the service runs in a user-neutral mode, which isn't something Qt can do much about, although the Anrdoid package infrastructure might.
> Does the Service run as a different user than the user app ?

No. It is started with the same privileges and as the same user as the app. I'm really doing nothing more here than following Qt's own documentation on how to create an Android service by the example (and these examples also go into using a different process).
> Is "the activity" what I would think of as a user app ?

It seems like you really don't know much about the Android architecture as this is one of the first terms one learns when dealing with Android at all. But your suspicion is correct,, the activity is basically the UI.

> In so far as that's a decent model of what's happening, I can imagine the Android O/S layer may treat the service as user-neutral and thus run it in a "vanilla" environment, with no user-specific customisations, thus in particular no localisation. …

No, that's not what's happening. One can also read the locale from a service context under Android. The problem is really that the platform integration plugin for Android only implements reading the locale in the presence of an activity.
> Why does the service need to do translations ?
> For example, if it's generating messages for the user-facing app to display, surely it could deliver the messages in a locale-neutral way and leave the app to do the translation ?

That doesn't make any sense. If I would ensure the activity (basically the full blown app) is started each and every time I want to update the text of a persistent notification users would be very unhappy about my app not staying properly in the background. Hence I don't even think Android allows this. Note that services under Android are often tied to a persistent notification so users know the service is running and it is the responsibility of the service to update that notification.
> although a
QCoreApplication
may well be required
Of course.
> and
QGuiApplication
is based on
QCoreApplication
, so perhaps what made it work for you was actually something in the base class.
No because `QAndroidService` is also based on `QCoreApplication`.
> You should be able, even without (or before you create) a
Q*Application
, to create a
QLocale
from its constructors taking some combination of language, script and territory, or taking a string identifying a locale …
At least the latter didn't work in my tests.
> Are you sure you asked for
QLocale()
, default-constructed, not
QLocale::system()
Yes, I'm sure I asked for the default constructed QLocale().
> the underlying problem is that the service runs in a user-neutral mode, which isn't something Qt can do much about, although the Anrdoid package infrastructure might.
That's surely
not

the problem. Qt has code to determine the locale reading the configuration of the activity context. The same code could run if a service context is present (instead of an activity). It just doesn't because the code is not structured that way right now - but it could be restructured with some work. And note that this is not only about detecting the current locale¹ but also that Qt's localization mechanisms only seem to work in the presence of a QGuiApplication under Android.

¹  As mentioned before, the lack of the auto-detection can be easily worked around by passing the current locale manually from the UI process. (An alternative would be querying the locale from the service context using custom Java/JNI/C++ code. To avoid reinventing the wheel one could just copy the Java/JNI/C++ code from Qt that is executed in the presence of an activity context and use it for the service context. This is of course not nice because one would duplicate code of Qt. Hence I didn't even bother to mention this when creating the ticket. I would also assume that the Qt devs developing the Android backend know this anyway.)
It seems like you really don't know much about the Android architecture
Indeed; I maintain
QLocale

and some other cross-platform components, but the platform backend for the Android system locale is part of the Android team's platform code, and I don't know much about individual platforms beyond the one I used daily and the one with most of the bugs, neither of which is Android.  Thanks for the education on a bit more than I knew previously about how things work on Android.
The problem is really that the platform integration plugin for Android only implements reading the locale in the presence of an activity.
I see.  That's what I needed to know then: it means this is really a ticket for the Android platform team.

No, that's not what's happening. One can also read the locale from a service context under Android. The problem is really that the platform integration plugin for Android only implements reading the locale in the presence of an activity.
From the code at
QAndroidSystemLocale

, the app's context is used, that can be an activity but if there's no valid activity it will use the service, so I'm not sure how that's not working properly. Could you perhaps share a snippet of your app's service code or project?

I realized shortly that the code handling this locale information is under the QPA plugin and since the service is a QCoreApplication, it doesn't really access that. So, the way to deal with this is to move that code outside of the QPA plugin, since it doesn't necessarily belong there, there's anything graphical about the locale and it should work with or without a GUI.

The code you linked would indeed work when executed for a service context. However, it is part of the Android platform plugin which is - as far as I understand - only loaded when instantiating QGuiApplication. Hence only with that I was able to make this work as mentioned in the ticket description; at least in one of my tests. So this code needed to be moved at a place where it can be executed without requiring the Android platform plugin because loading this plugin from the service process seems problematic; at least in one of my tests the service process got stuck.
This is my service code for the C++ side:
https://github.com/Martchus/syncthingtray/blob/d8a450c9a917648a8f18f8e91cdcd1a81d36d9f4/tray/application/main.cpp#L322
And this the code for the Java side:

items.fromString:
It seems that QLocale::system() and therefore also QLocale() don't return the configured system locale under Android when invoked from the service process. This in turn leads to translations not working there.

I therefore tried passing the QLocale().bcp47Name() from the frontend to the service manually where I would invoke QLocale::setDefault(QLocale(passedBcp47Name)). The last invocation was in my tests effectively QLocale::setDefault(QLocale(QStringLiteral("de"))). This also didn't work - QLocale() still got me the "C" locale and translations were not working.

I therefore tried instantiating a QGuiApplication in the service process with the help of a previous change of my which got merged: [https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/653832]

Only with this setting the default locale in the service process manually worked.

With this I got translations working but this approach has some serious drawbacks:
 # It shouldn't be required to pass the locale from the frontend to the service manually.
 # It shouldn't be required to instantiate a QGuiApplication in the service process for localization to work. (QAndroidService should be enough.)
 # Instantiating a QGuiApplication didn't even work in all my tests.
 ## It worked well with my x86-64 development build of Qt (with qtbase at {color:#b26818}5f6bfa3692a91c9f162606c25ec496656c253dfe{color}) in the emulator and Android 15.
 ## It didn't work with my aarch64 release build of Qt (version 6.9.2) on a real Samsung phone with Android 14 because the service got stuck up on the QGuiApplication instantiation leading to Android producing an ANR for the service process. Not sure why that is. When I tested [https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qtbase/+/653832] with Android 6.9.1 (or was it even still 6.9.0?) the icon rendering I used it for worked on the very same phone where it now gets stuck.
 ## So if using a QGuiApplication is supposed to be "the way" despite 1. and 2. then this needed to be sorted out. (For the sake of doing image processing/rendering it would also generally make sense to sort this out - but that's a different feature request.)

Note that my use case for this is updating an Android notification from the service process even if the activity process isn't running.

See codereview:
https://codereview.qt-project.org/c/qt/qt5/+/723731
Current blockers
Windows: Need to create new MSYS prebuilt package that contains 'nasm' package
Windows: Needs investigation regarding AV1 encoding error in QMediaRecorder test
All hosts: Needs fix for media duration calculation test (see Tim's patch)
Android: Hitting issues in auto-tests related to certain files being missing. Could be an issue androidtestrunner.
There are vulnerabilities affecting FFMPEG 7.x but fixed by 8.x. For example:
So I wonder what we will do the all the Qt versions prior to 6.12? Do we upgrade FFMPEG version packed with them? Is this considered “safety-critical” situation?
side note: the pack in question is in ffmpeg-7.1.5
The relevant patch is now in prestaging.

content.text: qtbridge build fails on docs.rs:
The build-log points towards an incompatible Qt version, in particular Qt5:

[INFO] [stderr] warning: qtbridge-type-lib@0.1.3: src/rustconv.h: At global scope:
[INFO] [stderr] warning: qtbridge-type-lib@0.1.3: src/rustconv.h:78:8: error: 'QSpan' does not name a type
[INFO] [stderr] warning: qtbridge-type-lib@0.1.3:    78 | inline QSpan<const T> RustSliceToQSpan(rust::Slice<const T> slice)
[INFO] [stderr] warning: qtbridge-type-lib@0.1.3:       |        ^~~~~

Option for fixing this could be to redirect to our own build, create a work around with build parameters and cfg or get into contract with the docs.rs admins. With minimal-qt we might be able to download the proper Qt version, if network access is available.
Added a post here asking for Ubuntu 26.04:
That would solve the issue in the most elegant way.
Under review here:
https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env/pull/202
